quiz.explain: The break-up and drift of Pangaea explains why continents are now where they are.
quiz.mistake: Thinks continents have always been fixed

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Were the continents always where they are now?'
teach.praise: One Pangaea in one Panthalassa, split into Laurasia and Gondwanaland! Gappu is drifting happily.
teach.nudge: Who proposed the theory, and what were Pangaea, Panthalassa, Laurasia and Gondwanaland?

topics.title: Evidence for drift: jigsaw fit, rock ages and tillite

learn.hook: Ancient glacier deposits are found in hot India and Africa today. Ice never formed there in the present climate, so the land itself must have moved.
points: Jigsaw fit: the facing shorelines of Africa and South America match remarkably. In 1964 Bullard used a computer programme to find the best fit of the Atlantic margins; the fit was almost perfect at the 1,000-fathom line rather than the present shoreline.
Rocks of the same age across oceans: radiometric dating shows that a belt of ancient rocks, 2,000 million years old, on the Brazil coast matches rocks in western Africa.
The earliest marine deposits along the coasts of South America and Africa are of Jurassic age, suggesting that the ocean did not exist before that time.

Tillite is a sedimentary rock formed from glacial deposits. The Gondwana system of sediments of India has counterparts in six landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere (Africa, Falkland Islands, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia, besides India).
Thick tillite at the base of the Gondwana system shows extensive, prolonged glaciation. It is clear evidence of past climates and of the drifting of continents.

example.q: Why was Bullard's 1964 fit done at the 1,000-fathom line and not at today's coastline?
steps: Present coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition.
The true edge of a continent is the continental margin, below sea level.
Matching at the 1,000-fathom depth line compares the real continental edges.
This gave an almost perfect fit.
example.answer: Because the 1,000-fathom line is closer to the true edge of the continents than the shifting shoreline.

learn.reallife: Talchir tillite in Odisha, part of India's Gondwana rocks, records an ice age when India lay much closer to the South Pole.

games.title: Evidence and what it shows

quiz.explain: Bullard's computer fit at the 1,000-fathom line was almost perfect.

quiz.explain: Tillite forms when glacial deposits are compacted into rock.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did Wegener prove the continents had moved?'

topics.title: Evidence for drift: placers and fossils; Wegener's forces

learn.hook: Ghana's coast has rich gold deposits but no gold-bearing rock nearby. The 'source' lies across the Atlantic, in Brazil!
points: Placer deposits: rich placer gold deposits occur on the Ghana coast, but there are no source rocks there. The gold-bearing veins are in Brazil, so Ghana's gold must have come from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
Distribution of fossils: identical land or freshwater species on either side of marine barriers need an explanation.
Lemurs occur in India, Madagascar and Africa, which led some to imagine a connecting landmass called 'Lemuria'.
Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow brackish water, is found only in the southern Cape province of South Africa and the Iraver formations of Brazil, now 4,800 km apart with an ocean between them.

Force for drifting: Wegener suggested the pole-fleeing force (linked to the earth's rotation and its equatorial bulge) and the tidal force (due to the attraction of the moon and the sun). Most scholars considered these forces totally inadequate.

example.q: Why is Mesosaurus strong evidence for drift?
steps: Mesosaurus lived in shallow brackish water.
It could not have swum across a 4,800 km wide ocean.
Yet its fossils occur in both South Africa and Brazil.
So the two areas must once have been joined.
example.answer: A shallow-water reptile could not cross an ocean, so South Africa and Brazil must have been connected.

learn.reallife: Grey slender lorises of Sri Lanka and India belong to the same primate group as Madagascar's lemurs, part of the puzzle that once inspired the 'Lemuria' idea.

teach.nudge: Explain the placer and fossil evidence, and why Wegener's forces were rejected.

topics.title: Post-drift studies: convection currents and ocean floor mapping

learn.hook: Wegener's big gap was 'What pushes the continents?' Two decades later, Arthur Holmes suggested the answer: the mantle is slowly boiling.
points: Convectional current theory: in the 1930s Arthur Holmes discussed convection currents in the mantle, generated by radioactive elements causing thermal differences. He argued that a system of such currents exists throughout the mantle.
Mapping of the ocean floor in the post-Second World War period showed that the ocean floor is not a vast plain but full of relief.
It revealed submerged mountain ranges and deep trenches, mostly located closer to the continental margins. Mid-oceanic ridges were found to be the most active in volcanic eruptions.
Dating showed that the oceanic crust is much younger than the continental areas.
Rocks equidistant from the crest of a mid-oceanic ridge, on either side, are remarkably similar in their constituents and age.

example.q: How did ocean floor mapping help revive the idea of moving continents?
steps: It found mid-oceanic ridges with active volcanism, i.e. a place where new crust may form.
It found deep trenches near continents, i.e. a place where crust may sink.
Ocean crust turned out to be young, and rocks matched symmetrically about the ridge.
These suggested the ocean floor itself is moving, leading to sea floor spreading.
example.answer: By revealing active ridges, trenches, young ocean crust and symmetric rocks: signs of a moving ocean floor.

learn.reallife: India's National Institute of Oceanography in Goa and the research vessel Sagar Kanya have mapped parts of the Indian Ocean ridges using similar techniques.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: Wegener proposed drift in 1912, while Holmes discussed mantle convection in the 1930s. R is true: convection offered a strong internal force to move crust.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order: Wegener (1912) came before Holmes (1930s)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'After Wegener, what new discoveries changed the story?'
teach.praise: Holmes's convection and the mapped ocean floor with young, symmetric rocks. Gappu is diving deep!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu about Holmes's convection currents and what ocean floor mapping found.

topics.title: Ocean floor configuration

learn.hook: The longest mountain chain on earth is not the Himalaya or the Andes. It is hidden under the oceans.
points: Based on depth and relief, the ocean floor is divided into three major divisions: continental margins, deep sea basins and mid-ocean ridges.
Continental margins form the transition between continental shores and deep-sea basins. They include the continental shelf, continental slope, continental rise and deep oceanic trenches.
Abyssal plains are extensive plains between the continental margins and mid-oceanic ridges. Continental sediments that move beyond the margins are deposited here.
Mid-oceanic ridges form an interconnected chain of mountains within the ocean: the longest mountain chain on the earth's surface, though submerged.
A mid-oceanic ridge has a central rift system at the crest, a fractionated plateau, and a flank zone along its length. The rift at the crest is a zone of intense volcanic activity.

example.q: A ship sails from the coast of Mumbai straight to the Carlsberg Ridge in the Arabian Sea. List the ocean-floor features it crosses in order.
steps: Near the coast: continental shelf.
Then the steep continental slope and the continental rise.
Then the deep, flat abyssal plain (deep sea basin).
Finally the mid-oceanic ridge (Carlsberg Ridge) with its central rift.
example.answer: Shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → mid-oceanic ridge.

learn.reallife: Mumbai High, India's biggest offshore oilfield, lies on the continental shelf, the shallow part of the continental margin.

games.title: Which division?
items: Area where continental sediments are deposited

quiz.q: The three major divisions of the ocean floor are:
options: Continental margins, deep sea basins and mid-ocean ridges
quiz.explain: Based on depth and relief, these are the three major divisions.
quiz.mistake: Lists only parts of the continental margin

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the continental margin?
quiz.explain: Continental margins include the shelf, slope, rise and deep oceanic trenches, not ridges.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every underwater feature is part of the margin

quiz.q: Extensive plains between the continental margins and the mid-oceanic ridges are called:
quiz.explain: Abyssal plains are the deep, flat areas where continental sediments settle.
quiz.mistake: Confuses them with shallow continental shelves

quiz.q: The longest mountain chain on the earth's surface is the:
quiz.explain: The interconnected mid-oceanic ridges form the longest chain, though submerged.

quiz.q: The zone of intense volcanic activity on a mid-oceanic ridge is the:
options: Central rift system at the crest
quiz.explain: The rift at the crest is where magma rises and erupts.

quiz.q: Where do continental sediments that move beyond the continental margins get deposited?
quiz.explain: Sediments carried past the margins settle on the abyssal plains.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sediments stay only near the coast

quiz.q: Deep oceanic trenches are included in which division?
quiz.explain: NCERT includes deep oceanic trenches in the continental margins.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Mid-oceanic ridges are the most volcanically active parts of the ocean floor.
Reason (R): They have a central rift system where magma rises.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The rift at the crest lets magma escape, causing intense volcanism.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the rift with volcanism

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is the bottom of the ocean just flat sand?'
teach.praise: Margins, abyssal plains and ridges with a volcanic rift. Gappu now sees the ocean floor in 3D!
teach.nudge: What are the three divisions of the ocean floor and what features do they have?

topics.title: Distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes

learn.hook: Plot every earthquake and volcano on a world map and they are not scattered randomly. They draw lines, and those lines outline the plates.
points: A line of earthquake dots runs through the central Atlantic Ocean, almost parallel to the coastlines, and extends into the Indian Ocean. It coincides with the mid-oceanic ridges.
In the Indian Ocean the line branches a little south of the Indian subcontinent: one branch goes into East Africa and the other meets a line running from Myanmar to New Guinea.
A second belt of concentration coincides with the Alpine-Himalayan system and the rim of the Pacific Ocean.
Earthquake foci along mid-oceanic ridges are at shallow depths, while along the Alpine-Himalayan belt and the Pacific rim they are deep-seated.
Volcanoes show a similar pattern. The rim of the Pacific is called the 'rim of fire' (Ring of Fire) because of its many active volcanoes. Map work: locate the Ring of Fire and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

example.q: An earthquake has a shallow focus and lies in the middle of the Atlantic. Another has a deep focus near Japan. Explain the difference.
steps: The mid-Atlantic quake lies on the mid-oceanic ridge, where plates pull apart; foci there are shallow.
The Japan quake lies on the Pacific rim, where one plate sinks under another; foci there are deep-seated.
So the type of zone decides the focal depth.
example.answer: Ridges have shallow-focus quakes; the Pacific rim (and Alpine-Himalayan belt) has deep-seated quakes.

learn.reallife: India sits next to the Alpine-Himalayan belt, which is why the Himalayan states and the North-East fall in India's highest seismic zone.

games.title: Shallow or deep-seated foci?

Rim of the Pacific near Japan
Ridge crest with plates pulling apart

quiz.explain: The Atlantic earthquake line follows the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

options: The rim of the Pacific Ocean with many active volcanoes
quiz.explain: The Pacific rim has a large concentration of active volcanoes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Alpine-Himalayan belt

quiz.explain: Ridge earthquakes have shallow foci; deep ones occur at the Pacific rim and Alpine-Himalayan belt.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all undersea quakes are deep

options: It meets a line running from Myanmar to New Guinea

quiz.mistake: Guesses a direction without recalling the map

quiz.explain: The Alpine-Himalayan belt is one of the two main belts with the Pacific rim.

quiz.explain: Volcanoes follow the same belts as earthquakes: ridges and the Pacific rim.
quiz.mistake: Thinks volcanoes and earthquakes are unrelated

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Earthquakes and volcanoes occur in definite belts.
Reason (R): These belts coincide with the boundaries of lithospheric plates such as ridges and the Pacific rim.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Plate boundaries are where crust is created, destroyed or strained, so quakes and volcanoes cluster there.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do earthquakes and volcanoes happen just anywhere?'
teach.praise: Ridges with shallow quakes, the Pacific rim and Himalaya with deep ones. Gappu can read the map now!
teach.nudge: Which belts have earthquakes and volcanoes, and where are foci shallow or deep?

topics.title: Sea floor spreading: the evidence

learn.hook: The ocean floor is like a giant tape recorder: as new rock forms at the ridges, it 'records' the earth's magnetic field, which keeps flipping.
points: Palaeomagnetic studies show that rocks on either side of a mid-oceanic ridge form parallel stripes of normal and reverse magnetic polarity, matching on both sides.

Rocks equidistant from the crest are similar in age, chemical composition and magnetic properties. Rocks closest to the ridge have normal polarity and are the youngest; age increases with distance from the crest.
Ocean crust rocks are much younger than continental rocks: no oceanic crust is more than 200 million years old, while some continental rocks are as old as 3,200 million years.
Sediments on the ocean floor are unexpectedly thin. If the ocean floor were as old as the continents, much thicker sediments would have collected.
Deep trenches have deep-seated earthquakes, while mid-oceanic ridges have shallow-focus earthquakes.

example.q: Rock A lies 10 km from a ridge crest and rock B lies 200 km away on the same side. Which is older and why?
steps: New crust forms at the ridge crest and moves outwards.
Rocks nearer the crest formed more recently.
Rock A is nearer the crest, so it is younger.
Rock B, farther away, formed earlier and is older.
example.answer: Rock B is older, because age increases away from the ridge crest.

learn.reallife: Indian scientists aboard ocean research cruises collect basalt from the Central Indian Ridge to date the youngest crust on earth.

games.title: Spreading evidence

Some oceanic crust is 3,200 million years old.
No oceanic crust is older than 200 million years; 3,200 million is for continental rocks.
Sediments on the ocean floor are unexpectedly thin.
This shows the ocean floor is young.
Magnetic stripes on either side of a ridge are mirror images.
They match in polarity, age and composition.
Ridges have shallow foci; trenches have deep ones.

items: Frequent volcanic eruptions at the crest

quiz.explain: Oceanic crust is young, nowhere older than about 200 million years.
quiz.mistake: Uses the age of the oldest continental rocks

quiz.q: Some continental rock formations are as old as:
quiz.explain: Some continental rocks date back about 3,200 million years.

quiz.q: How does the age of ocean-floor rocks change as one moves away from a ridge crest?
options: It increases and then becomes zero
quiz.explain: New crust forms at the crest and moves outward, so rocks get older away from it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ridge has the oldest rocks because it is highest

quiz.q: Rocks closest to the mid-oceanic ridge have:
options: Reverse polarity and are the oldest

quiz.explain: The newest rocks at the crest record today's normal magnetic field.
quiz.mistake: Assumes rocks near the ridge are the oldest

quiz.q: How many times older are the oldest continental rocks (3,200 million years) than the oldest oceanic crust (200 million years)?
steps: Oldest continental rocks = 3,200 million years

quiz.q: Unexpectedly thin sediments on the ocean floor suggest that:
options: The ocean floor is older than continents

quiz.explain: Little time has passed for sediments to pile up, so the floor must be young.

quiz.q: Normal and reverse magnetic stripes on either side of a mid-oceanic ridge are evidence from:
quiz.explain: Palaeomagnetism records the ancient magnetic field in rocks.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up continental drift evidence with sea-floor evidence

quiz.q:

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but thin sediments only show that the ocean floor is young. Trench earthquakes are deep because the ocean floor sinks deep into the mantle there.
quiz.mistake: Marks (a) whenever both statements are true without checking the link

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do scientists know the ocean floor is moving?'
teach.praise: Magnetic stripes, young rocks near the ridge, thin sediments and quake depths. Gappu is convinced!
teach.nudge: What do the magnetic stripes, rock ages and sediments tell us?

topics.title: Hess's sea floor spreading and the idea of plates

learn.hook: If new ocean floor forms at the ridges every year, the earth should be growing. It isn't. So where does old ocean floor go?
points: Harry Hess (1961) proposed sea floor spreading: constant eruptions at the crest of ridges rupture the oceanic crust; new lava wedges in and pushes the crust on either side, so the ocean floor spreads.

Because the spreading of one ocean does not shrink another and the ocean crust is young, Hess argued that the ocean floor pushed away from the ridge sinks at oceanic trenches and is consumed (subduction).
In the NCERT diagram, magma rises at the ridge, the floor moves away on both sides, and old floor sinks at a trench near a continent.
Plate tectonics was proposed in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker, and independently by Morgan.

A tectonic (lithospheric) plate is a massive, irregularly shaped slab of solid rock, generally made of both continental and oceanic lithosphere, moving horizontally over the asthenosphere as a rigid unit. The lithosphere is 5–100 km thick under oceans and about 200 km in continental areas.

example.q: Put Hess's model in order: crust sinks at trenches, magma erupts at the ridge, crust is pushed sideways.
steps: Magma erupts at the ridge crest and ruptures the crust.
New lava wedges in and pushes the crust to either side.
The floor moves away and finally sinks at an oceanic trench, where it is consumed.
example.answer: Eruption at ridge → crust pushed apart (spreading) → sinking and consumption at trench.

learn.reallife: The Andaman–Sumatra trench, where the Indian plate sinks below the Burma microplate, is the zone that produced the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

games.title: Sea floor spreading conveyor
items: Magma rises at the mid-oceanic ridge

Ocean floor moves away from the ridge
Old floor sinks at a trench and is consumed

quiz.q: Who proposed the hypothesis of sea floor spreading in 1961?
quiz.explain: Harry Hess proposed sea floor spreading in 1961.
quiz.mistake: Credits the earlier drift or convection scientists

quiz.q: According to Hess, the oceanic crust pushed away from the ridge eventually:
options: Piles up into mountains in mid-ocean
Sinks at oceanic trenches and is consumed
quiz.explain: Old ocean floor descends at trenches and is consumed, so the earth does not grow.

quiz.q: The concept of plate tectonics was put forward in 1967 by:
quiz.explain: McKenzie and Parker, and independently Morgan, proposed plate tectonics in 1967.

quiz.q: A tectonic plate moves horizontally over the:
quiz.explain: Rigid lithospheric plates move over the weak asthenosphere.
quiz.mistake: Thinks plates float on the core

quiz.q: The thickness of the lithosphere in continental areas is about:
quiz.explain: It is 5–100 km under oceans and about 200 km in continental areas.

quiz.q: Why did Hess think oceanic crust must be consumed somewhere?
options: The ocean crust is young and spreading of one ocean does not shrink another
quiz.explain: If crust were only added, the earth would grow; young crust everywhere meant old crust was being destroyed.

quiz.q: A tectonic plate is generally composed of:
quiz.explain: Most plates carry both continental and oceanic portions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each plate is either all land or all ocean

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In Hess's model the ocean floor spreads.
Reason (R): New lava erupting at the ridge crest wedges into the crust and pushes it on either side.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Continuous addition of lava at the crest pushes the existing floor outward.
quiz.mistake: Does not link ridge eruptions with spreading

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is sea floor spreading, and how is it related to plates?'
teach.praise: New floor at ridges, old floor sinks at trenches, all on rigid plates over the asthenosphere. Gappu is on a roll!
teach.nudge: Explain Hess's idea, including where the old floor goes, and what a tectonic plate is.

topics.title: Major and minor lithospheric plates

learn.hook: The earth's surface is cracked into about seven giant pieces and many smaller ones, slowly jostling like rafts on a pond.
points: Seven major plates: Antarctica and the surrounding oceanic plate; North American plate; South American plate; Pacific plate; India-Australia-New Zealand plate; Africa with the eastern Atlantic floor plate; Eurasia and the adjacent oceanic plate.

Important minor plates: Cocos (between Central America and the Pacific plate), Nazca (between South America and the Pacific plate), Arabian (mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass), Philippine (between the Asiatic and Pacific plates), Caroline (between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea) and Fuji (north-east of Australia).
A plate is called continental or oceanic depending on which occupies a larger part: the Pacific plate is largely oceanic; the Eurasian plate may be called continental.
It is the plate that moves, not the continent alone as Wegener believed. Continents are part of plates.
Palaeomagnetic data help reconstruct past positions of continents; the position of the Indian subcontinent (mostly Peninsular India) has been traced using rocks from the Nagpur area.

example.q: Locate the Nazca plate in words.
steps: Recall: Nazca is a minor plate.
It lies between South America and the Pacific plate.
So it is off the west coast of South America, under the Pacific Ocean.
example.answer: Between the South American plate and the Pacific plate, west of South America.

learn.reallife: India sits on the India-Australia-New Zealand plate, which is still pushing north into the Eurasian plate. This is why Delhi and the Himalayan region feel tremors.

games.title: Where is the minor plate?
pairs: Between Central America and the Pacific plate
Between South America and the Pacific plate
Between the Asiatic and Pacific plates
North of New Guinea, between Philippine and Indian plates

quiz.q: Which of the following is a major lithospheric plate?
quiz.explain: India-Australia-New Zealand is one of the seven major plates; the others are minor.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Arabian plate is major

quiz.q: The Cocos plate lies between:
options: South America and the Pacific plate
Central America and the Pacific plate
quiz.explain: The Cocos plate is between Central America and the Pacific plate.

quiz.q: The Arabian plate consists mostly of:
quiz.explain: NCERT describes the Arabian plate as mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass.
quiz.mistake: Links it with the Arabian Sea by name

quiz.q: The Pacific plate is largely a/an:
quiz.explain: Most of it lies beneath the Pacific Ocean, so it is an oceanic plate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every major plate is continental

quiz.q: How many major lithospheric plates are recognised?
quiz.explain: There are seven major plates.
quiz.mistake: Counts only continents or includes minor plates

quiz.q: Which statement reflects plate tectonics rather than Wegener's idea?
options: Continents alone plough through the ocean floor
Plates carrying continents and ocean floor move
quiz.explain: In plate tectonics the whole plate moves; Wegener thought continents moved alone.

quiz.q: The past position of the Indian subcontinent has been traced using palaeomagnetic data from rocks of:
quiz.explain: NCERT notes that rocks from the Nagpur area were analysed to trace India's position.
quiz.mistake: Picks a well-known region at random

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Eurasian plate may be called a continental plate.
Reason (R): A plate is called continental only if it carries no oceanic lithosphere at all.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: most plates carry both continental and oceanic lithosphere, and a plate is named after whichever portion occupies its larger part.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a plate must be purely continental or purely oceanic

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How many plates are there and which one is India on?'
teach.praise: Seven major plates, several minor ones, and India rides the India-Australia-New Zealand plate. Gappu is plate-perfect!
teach.nudge: Name the major plates, some minor plates and India's plate.

topics.title: Types of plate boundaries

learn.hook: Plates can pull apart, crash together or grind sideways. Each kind of meeting builds a different landscape.
points: Divergent boundaries: new crust is generated as plates pull away from each other. These sites are called spreading sites. The best-known example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the American plate(s) separate from the Eurasian and African plates.
Convergent boundaries: crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another. The place where a plate sinks is called a subduction zone.
Convergence can occur in three ways: between an oceanic and a continental plate; between two oceanic plates; and between two continental plates.
Transform boundaries: crust is neither produced nor destroyed; plates slide horizontally past each other.

Transform faults are planes of separation generally perpendicular to mid-oceanic ridges. They form because eruptions do not occur all along the crest at the same time, causing differential movement, and the earth's rotation also affects the separated blocks.

example.q: Classify each boundary: (a) Mid-Atlantic Ridge; (b) India pushing into Eurasia along the Himalaya; (c) plates sliding past each other along a fault crossing a ridge.
steps: (a) Plates pull apart, new crust forms → divergent.
(b) Two continental plates collide → convergent (continent–continent).
(c) Horizontal sliding, no crust made or destroyed → transform.
example.answer: (a) Divergent; (b) Convergent; (c) Transform.

learn.reallife: The Himalaya are a continent–continent convergent boundary, while the Andaman trench is an ocean–continent type of convergence affecting India's islands.

games.title: Boundary and behaviour
pairs: Plates pull apart; new crust created
One plate dives under another; crust destroyed
Plates slide past; crust neither made nor destroyed

games.title: Which boundary?
items: Ocean plate sinking under a continent
Two oceanic plates meeting and one subducting

quiz.q: At which type of plate boundary is new crust generated?
quiz.explain: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and magma creates new crust.

quiz.q: The location where one plate sinks under another is called a:
quiz.explain: Sinking happens in a subduction zone at convergent boundaries.

quiz.q: At a transform boundary:

quiz.explain: Plates slide horizontally past each other without creating or destroying crust.

quiz.q: The best-known example of a divergent boundary is the:
quiz.explain: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the American plates separate from the Eurasian and African plates.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three types of convergence?
quiz.explain: Convergence occurs between ocean–continent, ocean–ocean and continent–continent plates.

quiz.q: Transform faults are generally oriented:
quiz.explain: Transform faults cut across ridges, roughly at right angles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they run along the ridge

quiz.q: The collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate is an example of:
quiz.explain: Both are continental plates meeting along the Himalaya.

Assertion (A): Transform faults develop across mid-oceanic ridges.
Reason (R): Eruptions do not occur all along the crest at the same time, causing differential movement of plate portions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

quiz.mistake: Thinks spreading is uniform along the ridge

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What happens where two plates meet?'
teach.praise: Divergent creates, convergent destroys, transform slides. Gappu has the plate-boundary trio!

topics.title: Rates and forces of plate movement; drift vs plate tectonics

learn.hook: Plates move at roughly the speed your fingernails grow, yet over millions of years that adds up to whole oceans.
points: The strips of normal and reverse magnetic field parallel to mid-oceanic ridges help scientists determine the rates of plate movement.
Rates vary a lot: the Arctic Ridge is slowest (less than 2.5 cm/yr); the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, in the South Pacific about 3,400 km west of Chile, is fastest (more than 15 cm/yr).

Force: the mantle is slowly convecting. Heated material rises, spreads, cools and sinks back, forming convection cells. The heat comes from radioactive decay and residual heat. Holmes first considered this in the 1930s, and it influenced Hess's ideas.

Continental drift (Wegener): continents move, driven by pole-fleeing and tidal forces. Plate tectonics: lithospheric plates, carrying both continents and ocean floor, move over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection.

example.q: A plate moves at 5 cm per year. How far does it move in 1 million years, in km?
example.answer: 50 km.

learn.reallife: GPS stations of the Survey of India show the Indian plate moving north-east by a few centimetres every year.

items.q: 2 cm/yr for 100 years: distance in cm?
15 cm/yr for 10 years: distance in cm?
5 cm/yr for 1 million years: distance in km?
Fastest (15) minus slowest (2.5) rate, in cm/yr?

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the slowest and fastest rates, and what force drives the plates.

topics.title: Movement of the Indian plate

learn.hook: India was once an island near Australia. It then raced north across an ocean and crashed into Asia, and the Himalaya are the wreckage.
points: The Indian plate includes Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions.

Boundaries: the northern boundary is a continent–continent convergence along the Himalaya. In the east it extends through the Rakinyoma Mountains of Myanmar towards the island arc along the Java Trench. The western margin follows the Kirthar Mountains of Pakistan and extends along the Makrana coast.

India was a large island off the Australian coast, separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea till about 225 million years ago. It began its northward journey about 200 million years ago, when Pangaea broke.

About 140 million years ago, the subcontinent lay as far south as 50°S. The outpouring of lava that formed the Deccan Traps began about 60 million years ago, while India was still close to the equator.
India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago, causing rapid uplift of the Himalaya. The process continues and the Himalaya are still rising.

example.q: Arrange in time order: Deccan Traps begin, India near 50°S, collision with Asia, start of the northward journey.
steps: Start of the northward journey: about 200 million years ago.
India near 50°S: about 140 million years ago.

topics.title: Geomorphic processes and agents

learn.hook: The Himalaya are still rising, yet the Ganga carries away millions of tonnes of their rock every year. The earth's surface is a tug-of-war between building up and wearing down.
points: Endogenic forces (internal) build up or elevate parts of the earth's surface; exogenic forces (external) wear down relief (degradation) and fill up basins (aggradation). Wearing down of relief through erosion is called gradation.

Geomorphic processes are the endogenic and exogenic forces that cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials and change the configuration of the earth's surface. Diastrophism and volcanism are endogenic; weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition are exogenic.
A geomorphic agent is a mobile medium that removes, transports and deposits earth materials: running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves and currents.
Gravity is a directional force that activates all downslope movements of matter and also causes stresses on earth materials. All movements occur due to gradients, from higher to lower levels.

example.q: Classify as endogenic or exogenic: (a) uplift of a plateau; (b) a river carrying sand to the sea; (c) a volcanic eruption; (d) breaking of rock by frost.
steps: Endogenic processes come from inside the earth: uplift (a) and volcanism (c).
Exogenic processes act on the surface using external energy: river transport (b) and frost weathering (d).
example.answer: Endogenic: (a), (c). Exogenic: (b), (d).

learn.reallife: The Brahmaputra deposits huge amounts of sediment in Assam's valley (aggradation), while the Himalaya it drains are lifted by endogenic forces.

topics.title: Endogenic processes: energy and diastrophism

learn.hook: The heat that lifts the Himalaya comes from deep inside the earth: radioactive elements and heat left over from the planet's birth.
points: The energy from within the earth drives endogenic processes. It is mostly generated by radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, and primordial heat from the origin of the earth. Through geothermal gradients and heat flow, it induces diastrophism and volcanism.
Diastrophism: all processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the earth's crust.
Orogeny (orogenic processes): mountain building through severe folding, affecting long and narrow belts of the crust.
Epeirogeny (epeirogenic processes): uplift or warping of large parts of the crust. It causes simple deformation; it is a continent-building process, while orogeny is mountain building.

Diastrophism also includes earthquakes (local, relatively minor movements) and plate tectonics (horizontal movements of crustal plates). Diastrophism produces faulting and fracturing, and changes in pressure, volume and temperature that can cause metamorphism.

example.q: Distinguish orogeny and epeirogeny with one feature each.
steps: Orogeny: severe folding in long, narrow belts → mountains (e.g. Himalaya).
Epeirogeny: uplift or warping of large parts of the crust with simple deformation → continent building.
So the key difference is severe folding of narrow belts vs broad uplift of large areas.
example.answer: Orogeny = mountain building by severe folding of narrow belts; epeirogeny = broad uplift/warping of large areas (continent building).

learn.reallife: Hot springs at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and Bakreshwar in West Bengal are surface signs of the earth's internal heat.

topics.title: Volcanism and the exogenic processes

learn.hook: Push on a stack of books from the side and the top ones slide. Rocks feel the same 'shear', and that is how they start to break.
points: Volcanism (an endogenic process) includes the movement of molten rock (magma) onto or towards the earth's surface, and the formation of intrusive and extrusive volcanic forms.
Exogenic processes get their energy from the atmosphere, determined ultimately by the sun, and from the gradients created by tectonic factors.

Stress is force applied per unit area. It is produced in a solid by pushing or pulling and causes deformation. Forces acting along the faces of earth materials are shear stresses (separating forces); they break rocks and cause angular displacement or slippage.

Earth materials also face molecular stresses from temperature changes, crystallisation and melting. Chemical processes loosen bonds between grains. When stress exceeds a material's resistance, it breaks.
Weathering, mass wasting/movements, erosion and transportation are together called denudation, which means to strip off or uncover.

example.q: A force of 600 newtons acts on a rock face of area 3 m². What is the stress (force per unit area)?
steps: Stress = force ÷ area.
= 200 newtons per m².

learn.reallife: When engineers cut roads through hills on the Mumbai–Pune expressway, they study shear stress on rock faces to prevent slope failures.

topics.title: Climate, rocks and exogenic processes

learn.hook: The same granite crumbles in a different way in Rajasthan's heat, Kerala's rain and Ladakh's frost. Climate decides which exogenic processes rule.
points: Exogenic processes depend on the type of climate. Temperature and precipitation are the two most important climatic elements controlling them.
Vegetation density and type, which depend on precipitation and temperature, also influence exogenic processes indirectly.

Within a climatic region, there are local variations due to altitude, aspect (north- vs south-facing slopes receiving different insolation), wind speed and direction, rainfall intensity, and freeze-thaw cycles.
Rock type and structure matter too: differences in rocks lead to differential erosion, so soft rocks wear away faster than hard ones.
NCERT's diagram shows denudational processes (weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation) together with the driving forces behind them, such as solar energy, gravity and gradients.

example.q: Two slopes of the same hill in the mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere face north and south. Why might exogenic processes differ on them?
steps: The south-facing slope receives more sunlight (insolation).
It is warmer and drier; the north-facing slope is cooler and moister.
Different temperature and moisture lead to different weathering and vegetation.
So aspect causes local differences in exogenic processes.
example.answer: Because of aspect: the sunnier south-facing slope is warmer and drier than the cooler, moister north-facing slope.

learn.reallife: In the Kumaon Himalaya, villages and orchards prefer the sunny south-facing slopes, while north-facing slopes keep denser, moister forests.

topics.title: Weathering: meaning, factors and significance

learn.hook: Without weathering there would be no soil, no forests and no bauxite for aluminium. Slow-motion rock breaking is the foundation of life and industry.
points: Weathering is the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks through the actions of the elements of weather and climate.
Very little or no motion of material takes place in weathering, so it is an in-situ or on-site process.
Weathering is controlled by many geological, climatic, topographic and vegetative factors. Weathering processes are grouped as chemical, physical (mechanical) and biological.

Significance: weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments, preparing the way for regolith and soils, and for erosion and mass movements. Forests and biodiversity depend on the depth of the weathering mantle.

Weathering helps in the enrichment and concentration of valuable ores of iron, manganese, aluminium and copper. When some materials are leached away, the concentration of the remaining valuable material rises, making it economic to mine. This is called enrichment.

example.q: A rock contains 20 kg of aluminium ore mixed in 100 kg of material. Weathering leaches away 50 kg of other material. What is the new percentage of ore?
steps: Original ore share = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
After leaching, total = 100 − 50 = 50 kg; ore is still 20 kg.
Ore concentration has doubled: enrichment.
example.answer: 40%, the ore has been enriched by weathering.

learn.reallife: India's bauxite deposits in Odisha and Jharkhand, the source of aluminium, formed by intense weathering that removed other minerals and concentrated aluminium.

topics.title: Chemical weathering processes

learn.hook: Rainwater is slightly acidic. Given enough time, it can dissolve whole caves out of limestone.
points: Chemical weathering processes include solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. They act on rocks to decompose, dissolve or reduce them to fine particles, with water and air and heat speeding them up.

Solution: minerals dissolve in water or acids. Nitrates, sulphates and potassium are very soluble; common salt (sodium chloride) also dissolves. Calcium carbonate and calcium magnesium bicarbonate in limestones dissolve in water containing carbonic acid.

Carbonation: the reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate with minerals. Carbon dioxide from the air and soil air dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, a weak acid, which dissolves calcium and magnesium carbonates. This helps form caves.

Hydration: chemical addition of water. Minerals take up water and expand, increasing volume. Calcium sulphate takes in water and turns into gypsum, which is more unstable. Repeated hydration causes fatigue in rocks and may lead to disintegration.

Oxidation: combination of a mineral with oxygen to form oxides or hydroxides, where air and oxygenated water are available; iron, manganese and sulphur are commonly involved (rusting of iron is an example). Reduction occurs when oxidised minerals are placed where oxygen is absent, e.g. below the water table or in waterlogged ground.

example.q: Identify the process: (a) limestone dissolving in rainwater containing CO₂; (b) calcium sulphate becoming gypsum; (c) iron minerals in a rock rusting.
steps: (a) CO₂ + water → carbonic acid, which dissolves carbonates → carbonation.
(b) Addition of water to a mineral → hydration.
(c) Combination with oxygen → oxidation.
example.answer: (a) Carbonation; (b) Hydration; (c) Oxidation.

learn.reallife: The limestone caves of Borra (Andhra Pradesh) and Mawsmai (Meghalaya) were dissolved out by carbonation over thousands of years.

topics.title: Physical weathering: unloading, temperature and exfoliation

learn.hook: The smooth, rounded granite domes and boulders of the Deccan look polished, but no one polished them. The rock peeled itself like an onion.
points: Physical (mechanical) weathering depends on applied forces: gravitational forces (overburden pressure, load, shearing stress); expansion forces due to temperature changes, crystal growth or animal activity; and water pressure controlled by wetting and drying cycles.

Unloading and expansion: continued erosion removes the overlying rock load, releasing vertical pressure. The upper layers expand, and fractures develop roughly parallel to the surface. On curved surfaces this produces exfoliation sheets and large, smooth rounded exfoliation domes.

Temperature changes and expansion: surface layers expand more than deeper rock, creating stress that causes heaving and fracturing parallel to the surface. Differential heating and cooling leads to exfoliation and smooth rounded surfaces; in granites, rounded boulders called tors form.
Exfoliation is a result, not a process: it is the flaking off of curved sheets of rock. Exfoliation domes result from unloading, and tors from thermal expansion.

example.q: A granite hill has become a huge smooth dome after the overlying rocks were eroded away. Explain the weathering involved.
steps: Erosion removed the overlying load from the granite.
Pressure release allowed the upper granite layers to expand.
Fractures developed parallel to the curved surface.
Curved sheets peeled off (exfoliation), producing a smooth exfoliation dome.
example.answer: Unloading and expansion produced exfoliation, forming an exfoliation dome.

learn.reallife: Hampi's piled-up rounded granite boulders and the domes around Bengaluru are classic results of exfoliation.

quiz.mistake: Treats exfoliation as a process in itself

quiz.q: Fractures caused by unloading develop:
options: Roughly parallel to the ground surface
quiz.explain: Pressure release makes the upper layers expand and split parallel to the surface.

quiz.q: Which is a gravitational force involved in physical weathering?
quiz.explain: Overburden pressure, load and shearing stress are gravitational forces.

quiz.q: Why do surface layers of rock fracture during repeated heating and cooling?
options: Surface layers expand and contract more than the rock at depth
quiz.explain: Unequal expansion between surface and depth builds stress and causes fracturing parallel to the surface.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an expansion force in physical weathering?
quiz.explain: Expansion forces arise from temperature changes, crystal growth and animal activity.
quiz.mistake: Calls a gravitational force an expansion force

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Exfoliation domes are smooth and rounded.
Reason (R): Exfoliation domes form because rainwater chemically dissolves granite.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: exfoliation domes result from physical weathering, mainly unloading and expansion, which makes curved sheets of rock flake off.
quiz.mistake: Confuses physical exfoliation with chemical solution

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can rocks break without chemicals? And what is exfoliation?'
teach.praise: Unloading makes domes, heating makes tors, and exfoliation is the result. Gappu is cracking up with joy!
teach.nudge: Explain unloading and thermal expansion, and what exfoliation domes and tors are.

topics.title: Frost, salt and biological weathering

learn.hook: Water expands when it freezes, salt crystals grow in desert rocks, and tree roots push like hydraulic jacks. Small forces, repeated endlessly, crack mountains.
points: Frost weathering occurs due to the growth of ice in pores and cracks during repeated cycles of freezing and melting. It is most effective at high elevations in mid-latitudes, where freezing and thawing are repeated often; glacial areas face frost wedging daily. Rapid freezing causes sudden expansion and high pressure.

Salt weathering: salts in rocks expand due to thermal action, hydration and crystallisation. Salts of calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium tend to expand. High surface temperatures of 30–50°C in deserts favour salt expansion.

Salt crystals in near-surface pores split grains, which fall off: granular disintegration or granular foliation. Salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process, favoured by alternate wetting and drying.

Biological weathering: burrowing and wedging by earthworms, termites and rodents expose new surfaces to chemical attack; humans disturb vegetation and plough soils. Decaying plant and animal matter produces humic, carbonic and other acids. Plant roots exert tremendous pressure and break rocks apart.

example.q: Match each place to its most effective weathering: (a) high-altitude slopes of Himachal with daily freeze-thaw; (b) the hot, dry Thar desert with salty soils; (c) a forest where tree roots grow into rock cracks.
steps: (a) Repeated freezing and thawing → frost wedging.
(b) High temperatures and salts → salt weathering (salt crystallisation).
(c) Roots growing in cracks → biological weathering.
example.answer: (a) Frost wedging; (b) Salt weathering; (c) Biological weathering.

learn.reallife: Termite mounds in central India and earthworms in farm soils constantly rework the soil, exposing fresh material to weathering.

games.title: Which kind of weathering?

Granular disintegration in hot dry areas

quiz.explain: Repeated freeze-thaw cycles there make frost wedging very effective.

quiz.q: Why does rapid freezing of water in rock cracks cause weathering?

quiz.q: The most effective of all salt-weathering processes is:
quiz.explain: NCERT states salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process.

quiz.q: Granular disintegration in deserts is caused mainly by:
options: Salt crystals in near-surface pores splitting grains
quiz.explain: Growing salt crystals push grains apart and they fall off.

quiz.explain: Roots exert great pressure on rocks; this is biological weathering.

quiz.explain: Burrowing opens up materials so chemical weathering can act.

options: Calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium salts

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Salt weathering is common in deserts.
Reason (R): High surface temperatures and alternate wetting and drying favour salt expansion and crystal growth.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Desert heat (30–50°C) and occasional wetting help salts expand and crystallise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks deserts lack weathering because they are dry

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can ice, salt and tree roots break rocks?'
teach.praise: Frost wedging, salt crystals and busy roots and burrowers. Gappu knows the small rock-breakers now!
teach.nudge: Explain frost, salt and biological weathering and where each is most effective.

topics.title: Mass movements: causes, forms and slow movements

learn.hook: Ever seen electric poles on a hillside all leaning downhill? The soil beneath them is creeping, too slowly to see.
points: Mass movements transfer rock debris down slopes under the direct influence of gravity. Air, water or ice do not carry the debris; rather, the debris may carry air, water or ice with it. Mass movements do not come under erosion.

Factors favouring them: weak unconsolidated materials, thinly bedded rocks, faults, steep slopes, heavy rainfall and scarce vegetation. Activating causes include removal of support from below, increase in gradient and height of slopes, overloading (by materials or heavy rain and saturation), earthquakes, explosions or machinery, excessive seepage, drawdown of water from reservoirs, and removal of natural vegetation.
Three forms of movement: heave (heaving up of soils due to frost growth and other causes), flow and slide.

Slow movements: creep occurs on moderately steep, soil-covered slopes and is extremely slow and imperceptible; leaning fence posts and poles show soil creep. Types include soil creep, talus creep, rock creep and rock-glacier creep.

Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of soil or fine debris saturated or lubricated with water. It is common in moist temperate areas, where surface melting of deeply frozen ground and long continued rain occur.

example.q: After road widening on a Himalayan hill, the toe of a slope is cut away and heavy monsoon rain follows. Which activating causes of mass movement are present?
steps: Cutting the toe removes support from below.
It also steepens the slope (increase in gradient).
Heavy rain saturates and overloads slope materials.
Together these make mass movement likely.
example.answer: Removal of support, increased gradient, and overloading/saturation by heavy rain.

learn.reallife: Leaning trees and cracked retaining walls along hill roads in Uttarakhand and Sikkim are tell-tale signs of soil creep.

games.title: Activating cause or not?
items: Dense forest cover on gentle slopes

games.title: Slow movement terms
pairs: Extremely slow, imperceptible movement on soil-covered slopes
Slow flow of water-saturated soil or debris
Heaving up of soils due to frost growth

quiz.q: Mass movements are caused mainly by:
quiz.explain: Mass movements transfer debris downslope under the direct influence of gravity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an agent carries the debris

quiz.q: Why do mass movements not come under erosion?
options: The debris moves under gravity and is not carried by an agent
They do not move any material
quiz.explain: In erosion, an agent like water or wind carries material; in mass movement, gravity moves the debris itself.
quiz.mistake: Treats any movement of debris as erosion

quiz.q: Fence posts and telephone poles leaning downslope indicate:
quiz.explain: Imperceptibly slow creep of soil tilts objects over time.

quiz.q: Slow downslope flow of soil saturated or lubricated with water, common in moist temperate areas, is called:
quiz.explain: Solifluction is slow flow of water-saturated debris, often over frozen ground.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slow solifluction with rapid earthflow

quiz.q: The three forms of mass movement are:
quiz.explain: NCERT lists heave, flow and slide as the forms of movement.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an activating cause of mass movement?
quiz.explain: Vegetation holds slopes together; removing it, not planting it, triggers movement.

quiz.q: In mass movements:
options: Air, water or ice carry the debris
Debris may carry air, water or ice with it
quiz.explain: The debris itself moves under gravity and may carry water, air or ice along.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Indiscriminate removal of natural vegetation can trigger mass movements.
Reason (R): Vegetation binds slope materials and reduces saturation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Roots bind soil and plants reduce water saturation; removing them weakens slopes.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the stabilising role of vegetation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are mass movements, and why do slopes slip?'
teach.praise: Gravity-driven movements, triggered by steepening, rain and lost vegetation, from slow creep to solifluction. Gappu is grounded!
teach.nudge: Explain what mass movement is, some activating causes, and the slow types.

topics.title: Rapid movements and landslides

learn.hook: In the Himalaya, a single night of cloudburst can send a hillside crashing onto a highway. Why do the Himalaya suffer more than the Western Ghats?
points: Rapid movements are common in humid regions on gentle to steep slopes. Earthflow: water-saturated clayey or silty material moves down low-angle terraces or hillsides, often slumping into step-like terraces.

Mudflow: with heavy rain and no vegetation, thick weathered layers saturated with water flow down definite channels like streams of mud. They can engulf roads, bridges and houses, and occur often on slopes of erupting or recently erupted volcanoes. Debris avalanche: on steep slopes in narrow tracks, even faster than mudflow, similar to a snow avalanche.

Landslides are relatively rapid and perceptible movements of relatively dry material. Types: slump (slipping with a backward rotation), debris slide (rolling or sliding without backward rotation), debris fall (nearly free fall from a vertical face), rock slide (sliding of rock masses down bedding, joint or fault surfaces) and rock fall (free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope).
Debris avalanches and landslides are very frequent in the Himalaya because they are tectonically active, made mostly of sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated deposits, and have very steep slopes.

The Nilgiris and Western Ghats are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks, yet landslides occur there because of very steep slopes and cliffs, strong mechanical weathering due to temperature changes, and heavy rainfall over short periods.

example.q: A block of earth slips downhill and tilts backwards as it moves. Name the movement and contrast it with a debris slide.
steps: Slipping with backward rotation is a slump.
A debris slide is rapid rolling or sliding of debris without backward rotation.
So the key difference is the backward rotation.
example.answer: Slump (with backward rotation); a debris slide has no backward rotation.

learn.reallife: Landslides on the Konkan Railway during heavy monsoon spells show that even the hard-rock Western Ghats are vulnerable on steep cuttings.

games.title: Landslide types
pairs: Rolling or sliding without backward rotation
Nearly free fall from a vertical face
Sliding along bedding, joint or fault surfaces
Free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope

games.title: Why landslides happen here?
items: Strong mechanical weathering from temperature changes

quiz.q: A stream of water-saturated weathered material flowing down a definite channel is a:
quiz.explain: Mudflows are streams of mud moving along channels, often after heavy rain on bare slopes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses fast flows with slow creep

quiz.q: Which rapid movement is similar to a snow avalanche and can be faster than a mudflow?
quiz.explain: Debris avalanches occur in narrow tracks on steep slopes and are very fast.

quiz.q: Slipping of rock debris with a backward rotation with respect to the slope is called:
quiz.explain: Backward rotation is the defining feature of a slump.

quiz.q: Free falling of rock blocks over a steep slope, keeping away from the slope, is:
quiz.explain: In a rock fall, blocks fall freely through the air.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rock fall slides along the slope

quiz.q: Landslides involve materials that are:
quiz.explain: NCERT notes that landslides are rapid movements of relatively dry materials.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason for frequent landslides in the Himalaya?
options: They are tectonically active with steep slopes and unconsolidated deposits
They are made of very hard rocks and are stable
quiz.explain: Tectonic activity, weak sedimentary materials and steep slopes make the Himalaya prone.
quiz.mistake: Uses the features of the Western Ghats

quiz.q: Why do landslides occur in the Western Ghats even though they are tectonically stable?
options: They are made of loose sand
Very steep slopes, strong mechanical weathering and heavy rain in short periods
quiz.explain: Steep cliffs, temperature-driven weathering and intense monsoon rain cause failures.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Landslides occur in the Western Ghats mainly because the region is tectonically very active.
Reason (R): The Western Ghats have very steep slopes and receive heavy rainfall over short periods.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the Western Ghats and Nilgiris are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks. R is true: steep slopes, strong mechanical weathering and intense short spells of rain are what cause landslides there.
quiz.mistake: Applies the Himalayan explanation (tectonic activity) to the Western Ghats

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What kinds of fast slope movements are there? Why so many landslides in the Himalaya?'
teach.praise: Earthflows, mudflows, avalanches, slumps and rock falls, plus why the Himalaya slide more. Gappu is on solid ground!
teach.nudge: Name the rapid movements and landslide types, and compare the Himalaya with the Western Ghats.

topics.title: Erosion and deposition

learn.hook: Weathering is a rock breaking at home. Erosion is the rock leaving home, on a river, a glacier or a gust of wind.
points: Erosion involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris. It is largely responsible for the continuous changes in the earth's surface.
Weathering is in-situ and involves no motion; erosion involves movement of material. Weathering aids erosion, but it is not a pre-condition for erosion.

Erosion and transportation are controlled by kinetic energy. The agents are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and groundwater; the first three are controlled by climate. Abrasion by debris carried by agents greatly aids erosion.

Running water is the most important agent in humid regions with heavy rainfall; wind operates mainly in hot dry deserts; glaciers work in high latitudes and high altitudes; waves act along coasts; groundwater is effective in limestone areas.

Deposition is a consequence of erosion: when agents lose velocity and energy on gentler slopes, they drop their load. Coarser materials are deposited first and finer ones later. Deposition is not the work of a separate agent.

example.q: A river slows down as it enters the plains from the hills. What happens to its load and in what order?
steps: Velocity drops on the gentler slope, so energy falls.
The river can no longer carry all its load and starts depositing.
Coarse material (boulders, gravel) settles first.
Finer material (sand, silt, clay) is carried farther and settles later.
example.answer: It deposits its load: coarse material first, finer material later.

learn.reallife: The Kosi drops gravel near the foothills and carries fine silt far into the plains of Bihar, a textbook example of sorted deposition.

games.title: Weathering or erosion?

quiz.q: Erosion involves:
options: Breaking rocks in place without movement
Acquisition and transportation of rock debris
quiz.explain: Erosion picks up and carries away debris.

quiz.q: The main difference between weathering and erosion is that:
options: Weathering involves movement, erosion does not
Erosion involves movement of material, weathering does not
quiz.explain: Weathering is in-situ; erosion transports material.

quiz.q: Erosion and transportation are controlled by:
quiz.explain: Moving agents use kinetic energy to erode and transport.

quiz.q: Which agent is the most important in humid regions with heavy rainfall?
quiz.explain: In humid regions, running water does the most geomorphic work.

quiz.q: During deposition by a slowing river, which material settles first?
quiz.explain: Heavier, coarser material settles first; finer particles travel farther.

quiz.q: Which statement about deposition is correct?
options: It is caused by a separate agent
It is a consequence of erosion when agents lose velocity
quiz.explain: Deposition occurs when an eroding agent slows and drops its load.
quiz.mistake: Treats deposition as independent of erosion

quiz.q: Of wind, running water, glaciers, waves and groundwater, which three are controlled by climatic conditions according to NCERT?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes that wind, running water and glaciers are controlled by climate.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Weathering is a pre-condition for erosion.
Reason (R): Weathering aids erosion by breaking rocks into smaller fragments.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: NCERT says weathering aids erosion but is not a pre-condition for it. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't erosion the same as weathering? And where does all the eroded stuff go?'
teach.praise: Weathering stays home, erosion travels, and deposition drops the load as agents slow. Gappu has it!

topics.title: Soil formation: process, profile, parent material and topography

learn.hook: A handful of good soil can take centuries to form, and it starts with bacteria, lichens and mosses settling on broken rock.
points: Soil is a collection of natural bodies on the earth's surface containing living matter and supporting or capable of supporting plants. It is a dynamic medium with constant chemical, physical and biological activity.

Soil formation (pedogenesis) depends first on weathering; the weathering mantle is the basic input. Weathered material or transported deposits are colonised by bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens; dead remains build humus; grasses, ferns, bushes and trees follow. Roots and burrowing animals make it porous; a mature soil, a mix of mineral and organic products, forms and develops layers (horizons) seen in a soil profile.
Five soil-forming factors: parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time. They act together.

Parent material is a passive control factor. It can be in-situ weathered rock debris (residual soils) or transported deposits (transported soils). Texture, structure and mineral composition of the debris matter.

Topography is another passive factor: soils are thin on steep slopes and thick on flat uplands; gentle slopes with slow erosion and good percolation favour soil formation. In middle latitudes, sunny south-facing slopes and cool, moist north-facing slopes develop different soils and vegetation.

example.q: Why is soil usually thin on a steep hillside but thick on a flat upland?
steps: On steep slopes, erosion removes weathered material quickly.
Water runs off instead of percolating, so less weathering at depth.
On flat uplands, material stays in place and water percolates well.
So soil accumulates and becomes thick.
example.answer: Steep slopes lose material to erosion; flat uplands retain it, so soil is thicker there.

learn.reallife: Alluvial soils of the Ganga plain are transported soils, while the black soils of the Deccan formed in place from basalt: residual soils.

quiz.explain: Pedogenesis depends first on weathered material.

quiz.explain: Bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens come first.

quiz.q: Soils formed from in-situ weathered rock debris are called:
quiz.explain: In-situ weathered parent material forms residual soils.

quiz.q: How many basic soil-forming factors are recognised?
quiz.explain: Parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time.

quiz.q: Soils on steep slopes are usually:
quiz.explain: Erosion removes material quickly on steep slopes.

quiz.q: Parent material and topography are described in NCERT as:
quiz.explain: NCERT calls parent material and topography passive control factors in soil formation.

quiz.q: Soil is called a dynamic medium because:
options: It is made only of rock
Chemical, physical and biological activities go on in it constantly
quiz.explain: Constant activity keeps soil changing.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Gentle slopes are favourable for soil formation.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

topics.title: Soil formation: climate, biological activity and time

learn.hook: The same parent rock can give a deep red soil in Kerala and a thin, stony soil in Ladakh. Climate, life and time make the difference.
points: Climate is an important active factor: moisture (intensity, frequency and duration of precipitation; evaporation; humidity) and temperature (seasonal and daily variation).

Excess water moves soil components downward (eluviation) and deposits them below (illuviation). In wet equatorial areas, calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and much of the silica are removed; removal of silica is desilication. In dry climates, evaporation exceeds precipitation, groundwater rises by capillary action and leaves salts that form a crust called hardpan. In tropical areas with intermediate rainfall, calcium carbonate nodules (kanker) form.
Higher temperature increases chemical activity (except carbonation), so tropical soils have deeper profiles; in frozen tundra, soils are mainly mechanically broken material.

Biological activity: vegetation and organisms add organic matter, moisture retention and nitrogen. Dead plants give humus. In cold climates, slow bacterial activity lets humus and peat accumulate; in humid tropics, intense bacterial action leaves low humus. Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants fix nitrogen. Earthworms, ants, termites and rodents rework the soil.

Time: the length of time soil-forming processes operate determines maturity and profile development. Soils on recent alluvium or glacial till are young, with no or poorly developed horizons. No fixed absolute time can be set for soils to mature.

example.q: Why do humid tropical soils have low humus even though plant growth is heavy?
steps: Humid tropics are hot and wet.
Bacterial growth and action are intense there.
Dead vegetation is rapidly oxidised (decomposed).
So little humus accumulates in the soil.
example.answer: Intense bacterial activity rapidly decomposes dead matter, leaving little humus.

learn.reallife: Farmers in India grow pulses like moong and arhar partly because Rhizobium in their root nodules fixes nitrogen and enriches the soil.

quiz.explain: Eluviation removes material downwards; illuviation deposits it below.

quiz.q: Removal of silica from soils in wet equatorial climates is called:
quiz.explain: Heavy rainfall leaches silica out of the soil: desilication.

quiz.explain: Rhizobium lives in nodules of legumes and fixes nitrogen for the host plant.

quiz.q: Why does humus accumulate in cold climates?
quiz.explain: Slow bacterial activity means organic matter decomposes slowly and builds up.

quiz.q: Soils developing from recently deposited alluvium or glacial till are:

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Frozen tundra soils contain largely mechanically broken materials.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

topics.title: Landforms, landscapes and their evolution

learn.hook: A river valley in Uttarakhand, a sand dune in Jaisalmer and a sea cliff in Goa each have a life story: youth, maturity and old age.
points: After weathering, geomorphic agents such as running water, groundwater, wind, glaciers and waves erode, transport and deposit material, and in the process create landforms.
Landforms are small to medium tracts or parcels of the earth's surface. Several related landforms together make up a landscape, a large tract of the earth's surface.
Each landform has its own physical shape, size and materials, and is the result of certain geomorphic processes and agents. Landforms change slowly or quickly as processes and agents change.
Landform evolution means the stages of transformation of a landform or landscape. Like living beings, landforms pass through youth, maturity and old age.
Two aspects matter when studying landforms: the stages of development, and the processes and agents shaping them. Each agent produces its own assemblage of landforms.

example.q: Is the entire Indo-Gangetic plain a landform or a landscape? Is a single oxbow lake a landform or a landscape?
steps: A landscape is a large tract made up of several related landforms.
The Indo-Gangetic plain contains floodplains, levees, oxbow lakes and more → a landscape.
A single oxbow lake is a small tract with its own shape and origin → a landform.
example.answer: Indo-Gangetic plain = landscape; oxbow lake = landform.

learn.reallife: Tourism brochures for Himachal describe 'landscapes', but a geography field trip zooms in on each landform: a moraine, a terrace, a gorge.

quiz.q: Small to medium tracts of the earth's surface are called:
quiz.explain: Landforms are small to medium parcels; many related landforms make a landscape.

quiz.q: A landscape is:
options: A large tract made up of several related landforms
quiz.explain: Landscapes are large tracts consisting of related landforms.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a landscape is a single feature

quiz.q: The stages through which landforms are said to evolve are:
quiz.explain: Like living beings, landforms pass through youth, maturity and old age.
quiz.mistake: Uses seasonal or geological time terms

quiz.q: Each landform is the result of:
quiz.explain: Landforms owe their shape and materials to specific processes and agents.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a geomorphic agent that creates landforms?
quiz.explain: Running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind and waves create landforms; eclipses do not.

quiz.q: Landform evolution refers to:
options: Stages of transformation of a landform or landscape over time
quiz.explain: Evolution means the changes a landform passes through over time.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'evolution' in the biological sense only

quiz.q: The two aspects to consider while studying landforms are:
options: Stages of development and the processes of agents
quiz.explain: Both the stage and the shaping processes explain a landform.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Landforms do not remain the same forever.
Reason (R): Changes in processes and agents alter the shape, size and nature of landforms.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: As processes and agents change, landforms evolve.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the difference between a landform and a landscape? Do landforms grow old?'
teach.praise: Landforms make up landscapes, and they age through youth, maturity and old age. Gappu loves the life story of land!
teach.nudge: Define landform and landscape and name the stages of evolution.

topics.title: Running water: stages of a river landscape

learn.hook: Follow a river landscape through time and you see a young, energetic stream turning into a slow, meandering elder that has flattened almost everything around it.
points: In humid regions with heavy rainfall, running water is the most important geomorphic agent. It has two components: overland flow as a sheet over the land, and linear flow as streams and rivers in valleys.

Youth: streams are few with poor integration; they flow over original slopes in shallow V-shaped valleys with no or very narrow floodplains. Stream divides are broad and flat with marshes, swamps and lakes. Waterfalls and rapids may exist where local hard rocks are exposed.
Maturity: streams are plenty with good integration. Valleys are still V-shaped but deep; trunk streams have wider floodplains with meanders. Divides become sharp, and waterfalls and rapids disappear.

Old age: smaller tributaries are few, with gentle gradients. Streams meander freely over vast floodplains with natural levees and oxbow lakes. Divides are broad and flat with lakes, swamps and marshes; most of the land is at or slightly above sea level.
Over a long time, relief can be reduced to an almost plain, a peneplain, with low resistant remnants called monadnocks standing out.

example.q: A region has many well-integrated streams in deep V-shaped valleys with wide floodplains and sharp divides, but no waterfalls. Which stage is it?
steps: Many well-integrated streams → not youth.
Deep V-shaped valleys and wide floodplains with sharp divides → maturity.
Waterfalls and rapids have disappeared → maturity.
Old age would have very gentle gradients and vast floodplains with oxbow lakes.
example.answer: Mature stage.

learn.reallife: The upper Ganga near Rishikesh shows youthful features, while the lower Ganga in West Bengal and Bangladesh meanders across vast floodplains, showing old-age features.

games.title: Youth, maturity or old age?

Vast floodplains with oxbow lakes and levees
Land at or slightly above sea level

items.text: An almost plain produced by long erosion is a ___.

quiz.q: In which stage do streams meander freely over vast floodplains with natural levees and oxbow lakes?
quiz.explain: Old age is marked by gentle gradients and vast floodplains with meanders, levees and oxbow lakes.

quiz.q: Waterfalls and rapids are typical of which stage, where local hard rocks are exposed?
quiz.explain: Waterfalls and rapids exist in youth and disappear by maturity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks waterfalls persist into old age

quiz.explain: Monadnocks are resistant remnants rising above a peneplain.

quiz.explain: Running water flows as sheets over the land and as streams in valleys.

quiz.explain: The broad flat divides of youth disappear and divides turn sharp in maturity.
quiz.mistake: Uses the youth or old-age description

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Heavy rainfall supplies the water that makes running water dominant there.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a river landscape change from young to old?'
teach.praise: Young streams with waterfalls, mature deep valleys, old meandering floodplains, and a peneplain at the end. Gappu has the full river life story!
teach.nudge: Describe youth, maturity and old age, and what a peneplain is.

topics.title: Erosional landforms of running water

learn.hook: At Hogenakkal, the Kaveri squeezes through a deep rocky gorge. Upstream, pebbles spinning in eddies have drilled perfect round holes in the riverbed rock.
points: Valleys begin as small, narrow rills, which grow into long, wide gullies, which deepen, widen and lengthen into valleys. Types include V-shaped valley, gorge and canyon.

A gorge is a deep valley with very steep to straight sides, almost equal in width at the top and bottom; it forms in hard rocks. A canyon has steep, step-like side slopes, is wider at the top than at the bottom, and commonly forms in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks; a canyon is a variant of a gorge (e.g. the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River; the Kaveri gorge near Hogenakkal).

Potholes are more or less circular depressions on rocky beds of hill streams, formed by stream erosion aided by abrasion of rock fragments that rotate in them. Large, deep holes at the base of waterfalls are plunge pools; they help deepen valleys.

Incised or entrenched meanders are very deep, wide meanders cut in hard rocks. The loops formed on original gentle surfaces get entrenched due to erosion or slow, continued uplift; they indicate the status of the original land surface.

River terraces mark old valley-floor or floodplain levels. They are products of erosion: the stream cuts vertically into its own floodplain. Paired terraces are at the same height on both sides; unpaired terraces are on one side only or at different heights. Causes: receding water after peak flow, change in hydrological regime due to climate change, tectonic uplift and sea-level change.

example.q: Distinguish between a gorge and a canyon.
steps: Shape of sides: gorge has very steep to straight sides; canyon has steep step-like sides.
Width: gorge is almost equal at top and bottom; canyon is wider at the top.
Rock: gorges form in hard rocks; canyons commonly in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks.
example.answer: Gorge: straight sides, equal width, hard rock. Canyon: step-like sides, wider at top, horizontal sedimentary rock.

learn.reallife: The Gandikota gorge on the Penner river in Andhra Pradesh is often called the 'Grand Canyon of India'.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: terraces form when a stream cuts vertically into its own earlier floodplain, leaving the old floor as a step; wind plays no part.
