teach.nudge: Name the erosional landforms and how a gorge differs from a canyon.

topics.title: Depositional landforms: fans, deltas, floodplains and levees

learn.hook: Fly over Andhra Pradesh and the Krishna spreads into many fingers before meeting the Bay of Bengal, building land into the sea year after year.
points: Alluvial fans form when streams from higher levels break into foot-slope plains of low gradient. The heavy, coarse load is dumped as a broad cone-shaped deposit. Streams on fans shift and form many channels called distributaries. Fans are low cones with gentle slopes in humid areas and high cones with steep slopes in arid and semi-arid areas.

Deltas are like alluvial fans but form where rivers meet the sea. Unlike fans, delta deposits are very well sorted with clear stratification: coarse material settles first, finer silt and clay are carried farther. Distributaries lengthen as the delta grows into the sea (e.g. the Krishna delta).

Floodplains are major landforms of river deposition. The riverbed made of river deposits is the active floodplain; the floodplain above the bank is the inactive floodplain, with flood deposits (finer silt and clay) and channel deposits (coarser, from abandoned channels). Floodplains in a delta are called delta plains.

Natural levees are low, linear, parallel ridges of coarse deposits along the banks of large rivers. When floodwater spills over the bank, its velocity falls and coarse, heavy material is dumped next to the bank. Levees are high near the bank and slope gently away from it.

example.q: Why are deposits in a delta well sorted while those in an alluvial fan are not?
steps: A fan forms suddenly at the foot of a slope, where coarse load is dumped quickly → poor sorting.
A delta forms where the river slows gradually into the sea.
Coarse material settles first, finer silt and clay are carried farther → well sorted and stratified.
example.answer: The gradual loss of velocity into the sea sorts delta deposits by size; fans are dumped abruptly.

learn.reallife: The Kosi's huge alluvial fan in Bihar explains why the river keeps shifting its course, earning it the name 'Sorrow of Bihar'.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does a river drop all the sand and mud it carries?'
teach.praise: Fans at the foothills, deltas at the sea, floodplains and levees along the way. Gappu has dug up all the deposits!
teach.nudge: Describe alluvial fans, deltas, floodplains and natural levees.

topics.title: Meanders, point bars and oxbow lakes

learn.hook: On the plains of Bihar, the Ganga and its tributaries loop like a garden hose left on the floor. Sometimes a loop gets cut off and turns into a lake.
points: Meanders are loop-like channel patterns that develop over flood and delta plains. A meander is not a landform but a type of channel pattern.

Meanders form because of (i) the tendency of water on very gentle gradients to work laterally on the banks, (ii) unconsolidated alluvial banks with many irregularities, and (iii) the Coriolis force deflecting the flowing water.
The concave bank of a meander (cut-off bank) is a steep, eroding scarp; the convex bank has a long, gentle profile.

Point bars (meander bars) are sediments deposited in a linear fashion on the convex side of meanders of large rivers. They are almost uniform in profile and width and contain mixed sizes of sediment. As point bars build on the convex side, the concave bank erodes actively.

When meanders grow into deep loops, they may be cut off by erosion at the inflection points, leaving oxbow lakes. Natural levees (coarse ridges along the banks from floodwater spill) differ from point bars (mixed sediments on the convex side of meanders).

example.q: Differentiate natural levees and point bars.
steps: Location: levees are along the banks of large rivers; point bars are on the convex side of meanders.
Formation: levees form when floodwater spills over and slows; point bars form from deposition by flowing water along the inner bank.
Material: levees are coarse deposits; point bars have mixed sizes of sediment.
example.answer: Levees: bank ridges of coarse flood deposits. Point bars: convex-side meander deposits of mixed sediments.

learn.reallife: Kanwar Lake (Kabar Tal) in Begusarai, Bihar, is often described as a residual oxbow lake left by a meandering river.

teach.praise: Meanders from gentle slopes, point bars on convex banks, and oxbow lakes when loops are cut off. Gappu is loopy with joy!
teach.nudge: Why do meanders form, where are point bars, and how does an oxbow lake form?

topics.title: Groundwater and karst: erosional landforms

learn.hook: In parts of Meghalaya, a stream suddenly vanishes into a hole in the ground and reappears kilometres away. Welcome to karst country.
points: Groundwater does effective geomorphic work in rocks like limestone and dolomite, rich in calcium carbonate. The processes are mainly solution and precipitation (deposition).

Any limestone or dolomite region showing typical landforms produced by groundwater through solution and deposition is called karst topography, named after the Karst region in the Balkans, next to the Adriatic Sea.

Swallow holes are small to medium, round to sub-rounded shallow depressions formed on limestone surfaces through solution. A sinkhole is an opening more or less circular at the top and funnel-shaped towards the bottom; sizes range from a few sq m to a hectare, depths from under half a metre to 30 m or more.

Solution sinks form solely by solution. Collapse sinks form when the bottom of a sinkhole is the roof of a cave that collapses; the term doline is sometimes used for collapse sinks. Solution sinks are more common than collapse sinks.

When sinkholes and dolines join, long, narrow to wide trenches called valley sinks or uvalas form. The limestone surface is eaten into a maze of grooves and ridges called lapies, formed by differential solution along joints; lapies may turn into smooth limestone pavements.

example.q: A sinkhole has a circular opening at the top that funnels down, but its floor suddenly gives way into an underground void. What type of sink does it become?
steps: A sinkhole formed by solution alone is a solution sink.
If its bottom is the roof of an underground cave and collapses, it opens into the void.
That makes it a collapse sink, also called a doline.
example.answer: A collapse sink (doline).

learn.reallife: The Cherrapunji–Mawsmai area of Meghalaya has limestone with sinkholes and caves, a classic karst landscape in India.

topics.title: Caves, stalactites, stalagmites and underground drainage

learn.hook: Inside the Borra Caves of Andhra Pradesh, stone icicles hang from the roof while stone columns grow up from the floor, one drip at a time.
points: Caves form prominently where limestone or dolomite alternates with other rocks (shales, sandstones, quartzites), or where limestone is dense, massive and thickly bedded. Water percolates through cracks and joints, then moves horizontally along bedding planes, dissolving limestone into long, narrow to wide gaps called caves.
Caves usually have an opening through which cave streams are discharged. Caves with openings at both ends are called tunnels.
Calcium carbonate dissolved in carbonated water is deposited when the water evaporates or loses its carbon dioxide as it trickles over rough rock surfaces.

Stalactites hang from cave roofs like icicles; they are broad at their bases and taper towards the free ends. Stalagmites rise up from the cave floor, formed by water dripping from the surface or through the thin pipe of a stalactite above. Stalactites and stalagmites eventually fuse to form columns and pillars.
In karst areas, surface run-off often goes down swallow holes and sinkholes, flows as underground streams, and re-emerges downstream through cave openings, so surface drainage is scarce.

example.q: How can you remember which grows from the roof and which from the floor?
steps: StalaCtites hold tight to the Ceiling (C for ceiling).
StalaGmites rise from the Ground (G for ground).
When they meet, they fuse into a pillar or column.
example.answer: Stalactites hang from the ceiling; stalagmites rise from the ground; together they form pillars.

learn.reallife: The Borra Caves near Visakhapatnam and the Belum Caves in Nandyal district (formerly part of Kurnool district) are among India's best-known limestone caves, drawing thousands of tourists.

topics.title: Glaciers: erosion, cirques and horns

learn.hook: The holy Ganga begins as meltwater from the Gangotri glacier's snout at Gaumukh, a 'cow's mouth' of ice.
points: Glaciers are masses of ice moving as sheets over land (continental glacier, or piedmont glacier when a vast ice sheet spreads over plains at the foot of mountains) or as linear flows down mountain slopes in broad trough-like valleys (mountain or valley glaciers). They move slowly, from a few centimetres to a few metres a day, basically due to gravity.

Glacial erosion is tremendous because of friction caused by the sheer weight of ice. Material plucked from the land is dragged along valley floors and sides, causing great damage through abrasion and plucking.
Example: the Gangotri glacier's snout is at Gaumukh, where the Bhagirathi emerges. The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda join at Devprayag (Deoprayag) to form the Ganga.

Cirques are deep, long and wide troughs or basins with very steep concave to vertical walls at the head and sides, often at the heads of glacial valleys. After the glacier disappears, a lake called a cirque or tarn lake may form inside.

Horns form by headward erosion of cirque walls: when three or more radiating glaciers cut back until their cirques meet, sharp, steep peaks result. Narrowed divides become serrated or saw-toothed ridges called arêtes. The Matterhorn (Alps) and Everest (Himalaya) are horns.

example.q: Explain how a horn like the Matterhorn forms.
steps: Several glaciers radiate from a mountain top, each carving a cirque.
Each cirque erodes headward (backwards into the mountain).
When three or more cirques meet, only a sharp, steep-sided peak remains.
This pyramid-like peak is a horn.
example.answer: By headward erosion of three or more radiating cirques meeting at the top.

learn.reallife: Hemkund in Uttarakhand and many lakes in the Himalaya sit in glacial basins, while the retreat of Gangotri's snout is closely monitored as a sign of climate change.

quiz.explain: Both are glacial horns.

quiz.q: A vast sheet of ice spread over the plains at the foot of mountains is called a:
quiz.explain: NCERT calls such sheets piedmont glaciers.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Arêtes are broad, flat-topped ridges between cirques.
Reason (R): Divides between cirque walls get narrowed by progressive erosion.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do glaciers carve mountains?'
teach.praise: Heavy ice plucks and abrades, carving cirques, tarns, horns and arêtes. Gappu is chilled with excitement!
teach.nudge: Explain how glaciers erode and describe cirques and horns.

topics.title: Glacial valleys, till and moraines

learn.hook: A river carves a V. A glacier bulldozes a U. Look at a valley's cross-section and you can tell who made it.
points: Glaciated valleys are trough-like and U-shaped, with broad floors and relatively smooth, steep sides. They may contain debris, moraines and lakes gouged from the rocky floor.

Hanging valleys may lie at a height on one or both sides of the main glacial valley; their truncated spurs look like triangular facets. Very deep glacial troughs filled with sea water and forming shorelines in high latitudes are fjords (fiords).

Glacial till is the unassorted coarse and fine debris dropped by melting glaciers; its fragments are angular to sub-angular. Outwash deposits are washed down by meltwater streams; unlike till, they are roughly stratified and assorted, with somewhat rounded fragments.

Moraines are long ridges of glacial till. Terminal moraines form at the end (toe) of glaciers; lateral moraines form along the sides parallel to the valley and may join a terminal moraine in a horse-shoe shape.

Ground moraines are irregular sheets of till left over valley floors by rapidly retreating glaciers. A medial moraine lies in the centre of a glacial valley flanked by lateral moraines; it is imperfectly formed and may be indistinguishable from ground moraines.

example.q: Differentiate glacial till from outwash deposits.
steps: Till: dropped directly by melting ice → unassorted coarse and fine debris, angular to sub-angular.
Outwash: carried and deposited by meltwater streams → roughly stratified and assorted, somewhat rounded.
So the key difference is sorting and roundness, due to water transport.
example.answer: Till is unsorted and angular; outwash is sorted, stratified and rounded.

learn.reallife: Trekkers to Gaumukh walk over hummocks of moraine debris dumped by the retreating Gangotri glacier.

quiz.explain: Glaciers carve broad, U-shaped troughs.

quiz.explain: Fjords are drowned glacial valleys.

options: Unassorted coarse and fine debris dropped by melting glaciers
quiz.explain: Till is dumped directly by ice, so it is unsorted.

quiz.explain: Terminal moraines mark the snout's farthest position.

quiz.q: Lateral moraines form:
options: Along the sides, parallel to the glacial valley
At the centre of the valley
At the toe of the glacier
Beneath the glacier as sinuous ridges
quiz.explain: Lateral moraines lie along the valley sides.
quiz.mistake: Uses the position of a medial moraine

quiz.q: Outwash deposits differ from till because they are:
quiz.explain: Meltwater sorts and layers the material.

quiz.q: A valley that opens high up on the side of a main glacial valley is a:
quiz.explain: Tributary glaciers carve shallower valleys left 'hanging' above the main trough.
quiz.mistake: Uses a river or tectonic valley type

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Lateral moraines may join a terminal moraine.
Reason (R): Together they can form a horse-shoe shaped ridge around the glacier's end.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Side ridges curving into the end ridge make a horse-shoe shape.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What shape do glacial valleys have, and what are moraines?'
teach.praise: U-shaped troughs, unsorted till, outwash, and moraines of every kind. Gappu is glacially brilliant!
teach.nudge: Describe glacial valleys, till versus outwash, and the types of moraines.

topics.title: Eskers, outwash plains and drumlins

learn.hook: Some glacial landforms are made by rivers that once flowed beneath the ice, and they still point in the direction the ice was moving.
points: Eskers: in summer, meltwater flows on, along or through the ice and collects beneath the glacier, flowing like a stream with ice as its banks. Coarse material like boulders and blocks settles in this ice channel; when the ice melts, a sinuous ridge called an esker remains.

Outwash plains: plains at the foot of glacial mountains or beyond continental ice sheets are covered with glacio-fluvial deposits as broad, flat alluvial fans, which may join to form outwash plains of gravel, silt, sand and clay.

Drumlins are smooth, oval, ridge-like features made mainly of glacial till with some gravel and sand. Their long axes are parallel to the direction of ice movement. They may be up to 1 km long and about 30 m high.

The end of a drumlin facing the glacier, the stoss end, is blunter and steeper than the other end, called the tail. Drumlins form by dumping of debris beneath heavily loaded ice and indicate the direction of glacier movement.

Key differences: glacial valleys are U-shaped while river valleys are V-shaped; till is unsorted while alluvium is sorted; outwash plains are built by meltwater from glaciers while alluvial plains are built by rivers.

example.q: A drumlin's steep, blunt end faces north and its gentle tail points south. Which way did the ice move?
steps: The stoss end (blunt, steep) faces the oncoming glacier.
The stoss end faces north, so the ice came from the north.
The tail points in the direction the ice moved, i.e., south.
example.answer: From north to south.

learn.reallife: Geologists mapping old glacial deposits in Ladakh and Himachal use features like moraines and outwash to reconstruct how far glaciers once extended.

quiz.explain: Drumlins are mainly till with some gravel and sand.

quiz.q: Broad flat alluvial fans of glacio-fluvial deposits that join together form:
quiz.explain: Meltwater deposits beyond the ice build outwash plains.
quiz.mistake: Uses a river or desert term

quiz.q: Drumlins may measure up to about:

quiz.explain: NCERT gives up to 1 km length and about 30 m height.

quiz.q: Which is a correct difference between a glacial valley and a river valley?
options: Glacial valley is V-shaped; river valley is U-shaped
Glacial valley is U-shaped; river valley is V-shaped
quiz.explain: Ice bulldozes broad U-shapes; rivers cut narrow Vs.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Drumlins indicate the direction of glacier movement.
Reason (R): The blunt stoss end faces the oncoming ice and the tail points downstream.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Their asymmetric shape shows where the ice came from and where it went.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do eskers and drumlins look like, and how are they made?'
teach.praise: Eskers from sub-glacial streams, outwash plains, and drumlins pointing the way. Gappu is on a glacial roll!
teach.nudge: Describe eskers, outwash plains and drumlins, and how they differ from river features.

topics.title: Coasts: high rocky and low sedimentary

learn.hook: Goa's cliffs and headlands look nothing like the long flat beaches and lagoons of Odisha. India's two coasts behave in opposite ways.
points: Coastal processes are the most dynamic and hence the most destructive. Most erosion and deposition is by waves; storm waves and tsunami waves can cause far-reaching changes in a short time.
Two types of coasts: (i) high, rocky coasts (submerged coasts) and (ii) low, smooth and gently sloping sedimentary coasts (emerged coasts).

High rocky coasts: rivers appear drowned; the coastline is highly irregular and indented; hill sides drop sharply into water. Erosion features dominate: waves pound hill sides into cliffs that retreat, leaving wave-cut platforms. The west coast of India is a high rocky retreating coast.

Low sedimentary coasts: rivers extend their length by building coastal plains and deltas; the coastline is smooth with lagoons and tidal creeks; land slopes gently into the water; marshes and swamps may abound. Depositional features dominate. The east coast of India is a low sedimentary coast.
Differences in short: high rocky = submerged, irregular, erosion dominant, cliffs; low sedimentary = emerged, smooth, deposition dominant, lagoons, bars and deltas.

example.q: Why does the east coast of India have large deltas while the west coast has very few?
steps: The east coast is a low sedimentary coast where deposition dominates.
Large rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri bring huge sediment loads to it.
The west coast is a high rocky coast where erosion dominates and rivers are short and swift.
So deltas form on the east coast, not on the west.
example.answer: The east coast is a low sedimentary, deposition-dominated coast fed by large rivers; the west coast is high, rocky and erosion-dominated.

learn.reallife: Chilika and Pulicat lagoons on the east coast and the cliffs of Ratnagiri and Goa on the west coast are textbook contrasts.

quiz.q: Which type of landforms dominate along high rocky coasts?
quiz.explain: Waves pound the steep coast, creating cliffs and other erosional features.

quiz.explain: Depositional forms like deltas and lagoons dominate the east coast.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the east and west coasts

quiz.explain: Rivers deposit sediment and extend the land seaward.
quiz.mistake: Uses the description of rocky coasts

quiz.explain: Rocky coasts are indented with steep slopes into the sea.

quiz.q: Which pair is a correct difference between the two types of coast?
options: Rocky: erosion dominant; sedimentary: deposition dominant
Rocky: deposition dominant; sedimentary: erosion dominant
quiz.explain: Rocky coasts are eroded; sedimentary coasts are built by deposition.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Lagoons are common along the east coast of India.
Reason (R): The west coast of India is a high rocky retreating coast.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but a fact about the west coast cannot explain lagoons on the east coast. Lagoons form there because the low sedimentary east coast favours bars and spits that enclose water.
quiz.mistake: Marks (a) whenever both statements are true without checking the link

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do the west and east coasts of India look so different?'
teach.praise: Rocky, submerged, eroding west coast versus low, emerged, depositing east coast. Gappu can tell them apart!
teach.nudge: Compare high rocky and low sedimentary coasts with Indian examples.

topics.title: Coastal landforms: cliffs, stacks, beaches, bars and spits

learn.hook: During the 2004 tsunami, villages behind healthy mangroves and sand dunes on the Tamil Nadu coast suffered less. Coastal landforms are natural shock absorbers.
points: Erosional landforms: sea cliffs are steep (a few metres to 30 m or more). At their foot lies a wave-cut platform; when it is above the average height of waves it is a wave-cut terrace. Waves and debris lashing the cliff base create hollows that grow into sea caves; cave roofs collapse and cliffs retreat. Isolated remnants of the cliff standing off the shore are sea stacks.

Depositional landforms: beaches dominate depositional shores. Most are made of sand; shingle beaches have small pebbles and even cobbles. Beaches are temporary features. Behind the beach, sand dunes often form long ridges parallel to the coast.

An offshore bar is a ridge of sand and shingle in the offshore zone, roughly parallel to the coast. When it is exposed above water, it is a barrier bar. A barrier bar keyed up to one end of a bay, or attached to a headland, is a spit (e.g. spits in the Godavari delta).
When bars and spits nearly close the mouth of a bay, it becomes a lagoon, which gradually fills with sediment to become a coastal plain.

Offshore bars are the first buffer against storm and tsunami waves; then come barriers, beaches, beach dunes and mangroves. Disturbing the sediment budget or mangroves exposes settlements to storms and tsunamis.

example.q: Arrange the stages by which a sea stack forms.
steps: Waves attack the base of a cliff, forming hollows.
Hollows grow into sea caves.
Cave roofs collapse and the cliff retreats inland.
A resistant mass of rock is left standing off the shore: a sea stack.
example.answer: Wave attack → sea cave → roof collapse and cliff retreat → isolated sea stack.

learn.reallife: Kerala's backwaters (kayals) are lagoons behind sand bars, while the Sundarbans mangroves shield Kolkata's hinterland from cyclones.

quiz.explain: Sea stacks are remnants of cliffs or hills cut off by wave erosion.

quiz.q: A wave-cut platform occurring above the average height of waves is called a:
quiz.explain: NCERT calls such a platform a wave-cut terrace.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a depositional beach

quiz.q: An offshore bar that is exposed due to further addition of sand is called a:
quiz.explain: When an offshore bar shows above water, it becomes a barrier bar.

quiz.q: A barrier bar keyed up to one end of a bay is called a:
quiz.explain: Spits are attached at one end to a bay's headland.

quiz.q: Beaches made of excessively small pebbles and even cobbles are called:
quiz.explain: Shingle beaches contain pebbles and cobbles rather than sand.

quiz.q: The first natural buffer against storm and tsunami waves is formed by:
quiz.explain: Offshore bars absorb most of the force first, followed by barriers, beaches, dunes and mangroves.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cliffs are the first defence

quiz.q: A lagoon forms when:
options: Bars and spits nearly block the mouth of a bay
quiz.explain: Enclosed bay waters behind bars or spits become a lagoon.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Removal of mangroves can increase damage from cyclones and tsunamis.
Reason (R): Mangroves, beaches and dunes absorb the destructive force of storm waves.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Without these buffers, settlements take the full force of the waves.
quiz.mistake: Thinks mangroves have no protective role

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What landforms do waves carve and build along the coast?'
teach.praise: Cliffs, caves and stacks from erosion; beaches, bars, spits and lagoons from deposition, and nature's tsunami shields. Gappu is wave-wise!
teach.nudge: Name the erosional and depositional coastal landforms and how bars protect coasts.

topics.title: Desert landforms: wind erosion, pediments and playas

learn.hook: Deserts are not just sand. Rocky floors, lonely hills and dazzling salt flats like the Rann of Kutch are all carved by wind and sudden floods.
points: Wind is one of the two dominant agents in hot deserts; the other is running water as sheet floods after rare, torrential rain. Desert floors heat up quickly, creating vertical air currents and turbulent winds.

Wind causes deflation (lifting and removal of dust and small particles), abrasion (sand and silt carried by wind wearing down surfaces) and impact (sheer force of momentum when sand is blown against rock).

Pediments are gently inclined rocky floors close to mountains at their foot, with or without a thin cover of debris. They form by erosion of the mountain front through lateral erosion by streams and sheet flooding. The steep wash slope and free face retreat backwards (parallel retreat of slopes through backwasting), so pediments extend at the expense of the mountain.
An inselberg is the remnant of a mountain left after pediments extend backwards. High desert relief is reduced to low featureless plains called pediplains.

In basins surrounded by hills, a nearly level plain forms at the centre. When covered by shallow water for a short time, it is a playa; playas often contain salt deposits. A playa plain covered with salts is an alkali flat.

example.q: Arrange the stages by which a mountain in a desert becomes a pediplain.
steps: Streams and sheet floods erode the mountain front laterally.
A gently sloping rocky floor, the pediment, forms at the foot.
The slopes retreat backwards (parallel retreat), extending the pediment.
Only a remnant hill, the inselberg, is left.
Finally the area becomes a low, featureless pediplain.
example.answer: Mountain front erosion → pediment → parallel retreat → inselberg → pediplain.

learn.reallife: The Great Rann of Kutch turns into a shallow water body in the monsoon and a shimmering salt flat in winter, much like a playa and alkali flat.

games.title: Wind processes and desert forms

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a process of wind erosion?
quiz.explain: Wind causes deflation, abrasion and impact; plucking is glacial.

quiz.q: Gently inclined rocky floors close to mountains at their foot in deserts are called:
quiz.explain: Pediments are rocky floors formed by lateral erosion and sheet flooding.

quiz.explain: Playas form at basin centres and evaporate quickly, leaving salts.
quiz.mistake: Uses a glacial or river lake term

quiz.q: A playa plain covered up by salts is called:
quiz.explain: Salt-covered playas are alkali flats.

quiz.q: Deflation refers to:
options: Lifting and removal of dust and smaller particles by wind
quiz.explain: Deflation is wind blowing away fine particles.

quiz.q: Besides wind, which other agent is dominant in shaping hot deserts?
quiz.explain: Rare, torrential rains produce sheet floods that shape desert landforms.
quiz.mistake: Thinks deserts have no water action

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Pediments extend backwards at the expense of the mountain front.
Reason (R): The steep wash slope and free face retreat backwards through parallel retreat of slopes.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Backwasting moves the slope back, enlarging the pediment.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does wind shape the desert? Is it all just sand?'
teach.praise: Deflation, abrasion and impact, plus pediments, inselbergs and salty playas. Gappu now sees the desert's secret shapes!
teach.nudge: Name the wind processes and describe pediments, inselbergs and playas.

topics.title: Desert landforms: hollows, mushroom rocks and sand dunes

learn.hook: Barchans march across the Thar like crescent moons, their horns always pointing the way the wind blows.
points: Deflation hollows: persistent wind in one direction blows away weathered mantle or bare soil, creating shallow depressions. Deflation also creates small pits on rock surfaces. Wind-borne sand first makes shallow depressions called blow outs, some of which deepen into caves.

Mushroom, table and pedestal rocks: rock outcrops worn by wind deflation and abrasion leave resistant remnants polished into a mushroom shape (slender stalk, broad rounded cap), a table top, or pedestals.

Sand dunes form well in dry hot deserts. Barchans are crescent-shaped with points (wings) directed away from the wind, i.e. downwind; they form where wind direction is constant and moderate over a uniform surface. Parabolic dunes form where sandy surfaces are partly covered by vegetation; they are reversed barchans with the same wind direction.

A seif is like a barchan but with only one wing, formed when wind conditions shift; the lone wing can grow very long and high. Longitudinal dunes form when sand supply is poor and wind direction is constant: long but low ridges. Transverse dunes are aligned perpendicular to the wind; they form when wind direction is constant and the sand source is an elongated feature at right angles to the wind.
Exam practice: identify a landform from its description; explain river valley stages; contrast how limestone behaves in humid (karst) and arid climates; explain glacial and desert landforms.

example.q: A dune is crescent-shaped with its horns pointing east. From which direction is the wind blowing?
steps: In a barchan, the horns point downwind (away from the wind direction).
The horns point east, so the wind is blowing towards the east.
So the wind comes from the west.
example.answer: From the west (westerly wind).

learn.reallife: Shifting barchans near Jaisalmer can bury roads and fields, which is why shelterbelts and grasses are planted in western Rajasthan to stabilise moving sand.

games.title: Dune types

quiz.q: Parabolic dunes form when:

quiz.explain: Seifs have a single wing due to shifting wind conditions.

quiz.q: Dunes aligned perpendicular to the wind direction are:
quiz.explain: Transverse dunes lie across the wind.

quiz.q: Longitudinal dunes form when:

quiz.explain: Poor sand supply with a steady wind builds long, low ridges.

quiz.explain: Persistent wind removes loose material, creating deflation hollows.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Barchans form where the wind direction keeps changing from season to season.
Reason (R): A uniform surface and a steady wind let sand pile into a regular crescent shape.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: barchans form where the wind direction is constant and moderate. R is true; shifting winds give seifs instead.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up barchans with seifs, which form when wind conditions shift

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What different kinds of sand dunes are there, and what are mushroom rocks?'
teach.praise: Barchans, parabolic dunes, seifs, longitudinal and transverse dunes, plus mushroom rocks and blow outs. Gappu is a desert explorer!
teach.nudge: Describe the dune types and how mushroom rocks and deflation hollows form.

chapters.title: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere

topics.title: The atmosphere and its permanent gases

learn.hook: Climbers on Everest carry oxygen cylinders even though the air there has the same gases. The problem is how thin the air gets with height.
points: The atmosphere is the envelope of air around the earth: a mixture of gases, water vapour and dust particles. It is essential for life and protects us from the sun's harmful radiation.
Air is densely compressed near the surface; its density falls rapidly with height. About 99% of the total mass of the atmosphere lies within 32 km of the earth's surface.
Permanent gases by volume in dry air (NCERT table): nitrogen 78.08%, oxygen 20.95%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.036%, neon 0.002%, helium 0.0005%, krypton 0.001%, xenon 0.00009%, hydrogen 0.00005%.
The proportion of gases changes in the higher layers: oxygen is almost negligible at a height of 120 km, and carbon dioxide and water vapour are found only up to 90 km from the surface.

steps: Nitrogen = 78.08%.
Oxygen = 20.95%.
example.answer: 99.03%, so nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99% of dry air.

learn.reallife: Indian Air Force pilots flying at high altitudes use pressurised cabins and oxygen masks because the air gets too thin to breathe normally.

topics.title: Carbon dioxide and ozone

learn.hook: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.036% of the air, yet it helps decide whether the earth is cosy or overheated. Ozone, even rarer, guards us from sunburn and worse.
points: Carbon dioxide is meteorologically very important: it is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
It absorbs part of the terrestrial radiation and reflects some back to the earth's surface. It is largely responsible for the greenhouse effect.
The volume of other gases is constant, but carbon dioxide has been rising in recent decades, mainly due to the burning of fossil fuels, which has increased air temperature.
Ozone is found between 10 and 50 km above the earth's surface. It acts as a filter, absorbing ultraviolet rays from the sun and preventing them from reaching the surface.

example.q: Explain why carbon dioxide is called a greenhouse gas.
steps: Sunlight (short waves) passes easily through CO₂ to heat the surface.
The heated earth radiates long-wave terrestrial radiation.
CO₂ absorbs part of this radiation and sends some back to the surface.
This traps heat like the glass of a greenhouse.
example.answer: Because it lets incoming solar radiation through but traps outgoing terrestrial radiation.

learn.reallife: India's push for solar energy, electric buses and the National Action Plan on Climate Change aims partly to slow the rise of carbon dioxide from fossil fuels.

options: More sunlight would be reflected by CO₂
Less terrestrial radiation would be absorbed and returned to the surface
quiz.explain: CO₂ traps part of the heat radiated by the earth; without it, more heat would escape to space.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If carbon dioxide and ozone are so tiny in amount, why do they matter?'
teach.praise: CO₂ traps heat and is rising, and ozone filters UV. Small gases, big jobs! Gappu is impressed.
teach.nudge: Explain the roles of carbon dioxide and ozone and why CO₂ is increasing.

topics.title: Water vapour and dust particles

learn.hook: Without tiny specks of dust and sea salt floating in the air, there would be no clouds and no monsoon rain.
points: Water vapour is a variable gas that decreases with altitude. In warm, wet tropics it may be 4% of air by volume; in dry, cold deserts and polar regions it may be less than 1%. It also decreases from the equator towards the poles.

Water vapour absorbs part of the insolation and preserves the earth's radiated heat, acting like a blanket so the earth is neither too cold nor too hot. It also contributes to stability and instability in the air.
Dust particles come from sea salt, fine soil, smoke-soot, ash, pollen, dust and disintegrated meteors. They are concentrated in the lower layers, though convection can carry them high.
Higher concentrations of dust are found in subtropical and temperate regions, due to dry winds, compared with equatorial and polar regions.
Dust and salt particles act as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour condenses to form clouds.

example.q: Why do deserts get very hot by day and very cold at night, while humid coastal places do not?
steps: Water vapour acts like a blanket, absorbing and holding heat.
Deserts have very little water vapour (less than 1%).
By day sunlight heats the ground strongly; at night heat escapes quickly.
Humid places have more water vapour that holds heat, so the range is smaller.
example.answer: Low water vapour in deserts means little blanket effect, so they heat and cool rapidly.

learn.reallife: Dust storms from the Thar in May–June raise dust levels over north India, and sea salt from the Arabian Sea helps seed monsoon clouds over the Western Ghats.

quiz.explain: Dry winds in subtropical and temperate regions carry more dust.

quiz.explain: Cold, dry regions hold very little water vapour.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does air have water vapour and dust? Are they useful?'
teach.praise: Variable water vapour as a blanket and dust as cloud seeds. Gappu sees the value of tiny things!
teach.nudge: How does water vapour vary and why is it important? What do dust particles do?

topics.title: Layers of the atmosphere: troposphere and tropopause

learn.hook: Every cloud, every monsoon shower and every thunderstorm you have ever seen happened in the bottom layer of the atmosphere.
points: Based on temperature, the atmosphere has five layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.

The troposphere is the lowest layer. Its average height is 13 km: about 8 km near the poles and about 18 km at the equator. It is thickest at the equator because strong convectional currents carry heat to great heights.
The troposphere contains dust particles and water vapour, and all changes in weather and climate take place here. It is the most important layer for all biological activity.
In the troposphere, temperature decreases at the rate of 1°C for every 165 m of height (normal lapse rate).

The tropopause separates the troposphere from the stratosphere. Air temperature there is about −80°C over the equator and about −45°C over the poles; since temperature is nearly constant there, it is called the tropopause.

example.q: The temperature at sea level is 30°C. Using a fall of 1°C per 165 m, what is the temperature at a height of 1,650 m?
steps: Temperature = 30 − 10 = 20°C.

learn.reallife: Hill stations like Shimla and Ooty are cooler than the plains around them because temperature falls with height in the troposphere.

quiz.q: The average height of the troposphere is about:
quiz.explain: It averages 13 km, about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator.
quiz.mistake: Uses the polar value as the average

quiz.q: The troposphere is thickest at the equator because:
options: The equator is closer to the sun
Strong convectional currents transport heat to great heights
quiz.explain: Intense heating drives strong convection that lifts the tropopause.

quiz.q: All weather phenomena take place in the:
quiz.explain: The troposphere contains water vapour and dust, so all weather occurs here.

quiz.q: In the troposphere, temperature decreases at the rate of 1°C for every:
quiz.explain: NCERT gives 1°C per 165 m.

quiz.q: The air temperature at the tropopause over the equator is about:
quiz.explain: It is about −80°C over the equator and −45°C over the poles.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the equator and pole values

quiz.q: The temperature on the ground is 28°C. What would it be at 990 m height, using a fall of 1°C per 165 m? (Answer in °C.)
steps: Temperature = 28 − 6
quiz.mistake: Adds the fall instead of subtracting

quiz.q: The troposphere extends to about what height near the poles?
quiz.explain: It is about 8 km near the poles and 18 km at the equator.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The troposphere is the most important layer for all biological activity.
Reason (R): The air temperature at the tropopause is about −80°C over the equator.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the temperature at the tropopause does not explain why the troposphere matters for life. It matters because it holds water vapour and dust, and all weather happens there.
quiz.mistake: Marks (a) whenever both statements are true without checking the link

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the troposphere, and why does it get colder as I fly higher?'
teach.praise: The 13-km-high weather layer, colder by 1°C every 165 m, capped by the tropopause. Gappu is flying high!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the height of the troposphere, its lapse rate and why weather happens there.

topics.title: Stratosphere, mesosphere, ionosphere and exosphere

learn.hook: Your AM radio can hear stations from far away at night because a layer 80 km up bounces radio waves back to earth.
points: The stratosphere lies above the tropopause and extends up to 50 km. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation and shields life from this intense, harmful energy.
The mesosphere lies above the stratosphere up to 80 km. Here temperature again decreases with altitude, reaching −100°C at 80 km. Its upper limit is the mesopause.

The ionosphere lies between 80 and 400 km, above the mesopause. It contains electrically charged particles called ions. Radio waves transmitted from the earth are reflected back by this layer. Temperature here increases with height. (NCERT lists this layer as the thermosphere in the five-layer division.)
The exosphere is the uppermost layer, above the thermosphere. Very little is known about it; its contents are extremely rarefied and it gradually merges with outer space.

Diagram practice: draw the layers with heights (troposphere up to about 13 km average, stratosphere to 50 km, mesosphere to 80 km, ionosphere 80–400 km, exosphere above) and the temperature trend in each.

example.q: In which layers does temperature fall with height, and in which does it rise?
steps: Troposphere: falls with height.
Stratosphere: contains ozone, which absorbs UV (temperature does not fall like the troposphere).
Mesosphere: falls again, to −100°C at 80 km.
Ionosphere/thermosphere: rises with height.
example.answer: Falls in the troposphere and mesosphere; rises in the ionosphere (thermosphere).

learn.reallife: Long-distance radio broadcasts, such as All India Radio's short-wave services, depend on the ionosphere reflecting signals back to earth.

topics.title: Elements of weather and climate

learn.hook: When IMD forecasts '38°C, humid, light winds, chance of thundershowers', it is describing the elements of weather.
points: The main elements of weather and climate are temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation. Each is studied in detail in the following chapters.
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place over a short time; climate is the average weather over a long period. Both are described using the same elements.
These elements interact: temperature affects pressure, pressure differences cause winds, winds carry moisture, and humidity leads to clouds and precipitation.

Exam focus for this chapter: percentages of gases, the layers of the atmosphere and their heights, the importance of water vapour and dust, why the troposphere is the most important layer, and the role of ozone.

example.q: Identify the elements of weather in this forecast: 'Delhi: 41°C, 996 hPa, hot westerly loo winds at 25 km/h, humidity 15%, clear skies, no rain.'
steps: 41°C → temperature.
996 hPa → pressure.
Loo winds at 25 km/h → winds.
Humidity 15% → humidity.
Clear skies → clouds; no rain → precipitation.
example.answer: Temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation.

learn.reallife: Farmers check IMD's agromet advisories, which use these elements to decide when to sow, spray or harvest.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of weather and climate?
quiz.explain: Latitude is a control of climate, not an element. The elements are temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation.

quiz.explain: Climate is long-term average weather; weather is short-term.

quiz.q: Pressure differences in the atmosphere mainly cause:
quiz.explain: Air moves from high to low pressure, creating winds.

quiz.q: In which layer do all six elements of weather operate?
quiz.explain: Weather, including clouds and precipitation, occurs in the troposphere.
quiz.mistake: Places weather in a higher layer

quiz.q: The instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure is the:
quiz.explain: A barometer measures air pressure.
quiz.mistake: Picks the instrument for another element

quiz.q: Which element is directly linked with water vapour in the air?
quiz.explain: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct sequence of linked weather elements?
quiz.explain: Heating changes pressure, and pressure differences cause winds.

Assertion (A): Precipitation depends on humidity and clouds.
Reason (R): Water vapour condenses to form clouds, from which precipitation falls.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Moisture in the air condenses into clouds, which then produce precipitation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks precipitation is independent of moisture

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly do weather reports describe?'

chapters.title: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

topics.title: Insolation, aphelion and perihelion

learn.hook: Here's a surprise: the earth is closest to the sun in January, yet that is when Delhi shivers in winter.
points: The energy received by the earth from the sun is called incoming solar radiation, or insolation. The earth's surface receives most of it in short wavelengths.
Because the earth is a geoid resembling a sphere, the sun's rays fall obliquely at the top of the atmosphere, and the earth intercepts only a very small portion of the sun's energy.
On average, the earth receives 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute at the top of its atmosphere.

On 4 July the earth is farthest from the sun (152 million km): aphelion. On 3 January it is nearest (147 million km): perihelion. So annual insolation received on 3 January is slightly more than on 4 July.
This variation is masked by other factors such as the distribution of land and sea and atmospheric circulation, so it has no great effect on daily weather.

example.q: How much closer to the sun is the earth at perihelion than at aphelion?
steps: Aphelion distance = 152 million km.
Perihelion distance = 147 million km.
Difference = 152 − 147 = 5 million km.
example.answer: 5 million km closer at perihelion (3 January).

learn.reallife: ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory measures the sun's output from space, above the atmosphere, where insolation is not reduced by clouds or dust.

topics.title: Why insolation varies: axis, angle and day length

learn.hook: Shine a torch straight down and you get a small bright circle; tilt it and the light spreads into a dim oval. That is why the poles are cold.
points: The amount and intensity of insolation vary during a day, a season and a year. The factors are: (i) rotation of the earth on its axis, (ii) angle of inclination of the sun's rays, (iii) length of the day, (iv) transparency of the atmosphere, (v) configuration of land in terms of its aspect. The last two have less influence.
The earth's axis makes an angle of 66½° with the plane of its orbit around the sun. This greatly influences the insolation received at different latitudes.
The angle of the sun's rays depends on latitude. The higher the latitude, the smaller the angle the rays make with the surface, giving slant rays.
Slant rays spread over a larger area than vertical rays, so energy per unit area falls. They also pass through a greater depth of atmosphere, causing more absorption, scattering and diffusion.

example.q: The earth's axis makes 66½° with the plane of its orbit. What angle does it make with the perpendicular to that plane?
steps: The perpendicular makes 90° with the plane.
Tilt from the perpendicular = 90° − 66½°.

learn.reallife: Solar panels in Ladakh are tilted at a steeper angle than those in Tamil Nadu so that the sun's rays strike them more directly.

quiz.q: The angle of inclination of the sun's rays depends mainly on:
quiz.explain: The higher the latitude, the more slanting the rays.

topics.title: Insolation through the atmosphere and its distribution

learn.hook: Why is the sky blue at noon and the sun red at sunset? Blame scattering by tiny particles in the air.
points: The atmosphere is largely transparent to short-wave solar radiation. In the troposphere, water vapour, ozone and other gases absorb much of the near-infrared radiation.

Very small suspended particles in the troposphere scatter the visible spectrum both to space and towards the surface. The blue colour of the sky and the red colour of the rising and setting sun are results of scattering.
Insolation at the surface varies from about 320 W/m² in the tropics to about 70 W/m² at the poles.
Maximum insolation is received over the subtropical deserts, where cloudiness is least. The equator receives comparatively less insolation than the tropics.
At the same latitude, insolation is generally more over continents than over oceans. In winter, middle and higher latitudes receive less radiation than in summer.

example.q: Why do subtropical deserts receive more insolation than the equator, even though the sun is higher over the equator?
steps: Insolation reaching the surface depends on cloudiness as well as sun angle.
The equator has thick clouds and heavy rain, which reflect and absorb insolation.
Subtropical deserts have the least cloudiness.
So more insolation reaches the surface in subtropical deserts.
example.answer: Because subtropical deserts have the least cloud cover, while the equator is very cloudy.

learn.reallife: Rajasthan's Bhadla Solar Park sits in the dry subtropics, where clear skies give some of the highest solar energy in India.

topics.title: Heating the atmosphere: conduction, convection and advection

learn.hook: In May, a scorching wind called the loo sweeps across north India and can push temperatures past 45°C. It is heat delivered sideways by advection.
points: The earth, heated by insolation, transmits heat to the layers of the atmosphere near it in long-wave form.

Conduction: when two bodies of unequal temperature are in contact, energy flows from the warmer to the cooler body until both reach the same temperature or contact is broken. Air in contact with land gets heated, and the layers above get heated by contact. Conduction is important in heating the lower layers of the atmosphere.
Convection: heated air near the surface rises vertically in currents and transmits heat upward. This vertical heating is convection; it is confined to the troposphere.

Advection: transfer of heat through horizontal movement of air. Horizontal movement is relatively more important than vertical movement. In middle latitudes, most diurnal variation in daily weather is caused by advection alone.
In tropical regions, especially northern India in summer, the local wind called 'loo' is the outcome of advection.

example.q: Name the heat-transfer process: (a) a warm road heating the air just above it; (b) a column of hot air rising over farmland on a summer afternoon; (c) hot loo winds blowing across Uttar Pradesh.
steps: (a) Heat passing to air in contact with the surface → conduction.
(b) Heated air rising vertically → convection.
(c) Heat carried horizontally by wind → advection.
example.answer: (a) Conduction; (b) Convection; (c) Advection.

learn.reallife: IMD issues heatwave alerts when loo winds carry desert heat across Rajasthan, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh in May and June.

topics.title: Terrestrial radiation, Planck's law and specific heat

learn.hook: The sun heats the ground, and the ground heats the air. That's why it's cooler on a mountain top even though it's closer to the sun.
points: Insolation in short waves heats the earth's surface. The heated earth becomes a radiating body and radiates energy to the atmosphere in long-wave form. This is terrestrial radiation; it heats the atmosphere from below.
Long-wave radiation is absorbed by atmospheric gases, particularly carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. So the atmosphere is indirectly heated by the earth's radiation.

The atmosphere in turn radiates and transmits heat to space. The heat received from the sun is finally returned to space, maintaining a constant temperature at the surface and in the atmosphere over time.
Planck's law: the hotter a body, the more energy it radiates and the shorter the wavelength of that radiation. That is why the very hot sun emits short waves and the cooler earth emits long waves.
Specific heat is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.

example.q: Use Planck's law to explain why the sun emits short waves and the earth emits long waves.
steps: Planck's law: hotter bodies radiate more energy at shorter wavelengths.
The sun is extremely hot, so its radiation is short-wave.
The earth is much cooler, so it radiates long-wave (terrestrial) radiation.
example.answer: The sun is much hotter, so it radiates at shorter wavelengths; the cooler earth radiates long waves.

learn.reallife: Thermal cameras used by firefighters and in airport fever screening detect the long-wave radiation that warm bodies give off.

topics.title: Heat budget I: reflection, albedo and absorption

learn.hook: Imagine the sun pays the earth 100 rupees of energy every day. Where does every rupee go? The heat budget is that account book.
points: The earth as a whole does not accumulate or lose heat; it maintains its temperature. This happens because the insolation received is balanced by the radiation sent back to space.

Take insolation at the top of the atmosphere as 100 units. About 35 units are sent back to space before reaching the surface: 27 units reflected from the tops of clouds, 2 units reflected from snow and ice-covered areas, and 6 units scattered to space.
The reflected amount of radiation is called the albedo of the earth.
The remaining 65 units are absorbed: 14 units within the atmosphere and 51 units by the earth's surface.

example.q: Check that the units add up: 35 units lost before reaching the surface and 65 absorbed.
steps: Lost: 27 (clouds) + 2 (snow and ice) + 6 (scattered) = 35.
Absorbed: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65.
Total: 35 + 65 = 100 units.
example.answer: 35 + 65 = 100 units, so all incoming insolation is accounted for.

learn.reallife: Melting Himalayan snow lowers the region's albedo, so the ground absorbs more heat and warms faster, a worrying feedback watched by Indian climate scientists.

topics.title: Heat budget II: terrestrial radiation and the balance

learn.hook: The ground absorbs 51 units. It gives them all back, but not all in the same way. Some go straight to space, some warm the air, and some ride up with evaporated water.
points: The earth radiates back the 51 units it absorbed, as terrestrial radiation.

Of these, 17 units are radiated directly to space. The remaining 34 units are absorbed by the atmosphere: 6 units absorbed directly, 9 units through convection and turbulence, and 19 units through latent heat of condensation.
The atmosphere absorbs 48 units in total (14 from insolation + 34 from terrestrial radiation) and radiates them back into space.
Total radiation returning to space from the earth and the atmosphere = 17 + 48 = 65 units, which balances the 65 units absorbed from the sun. This is the heat budget or heat balance of the earth.
NCERT's flow diagram shows these units moving between space, the atmosphere and the earth's surface.

example.q: Show that the heat budget balances.
steps: Absorbed from the sun: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65 units.
Surface gives back 51: 17 directly to space + 34 to the atmosphere (6 + 9 + 19).
Atmosphere radiates 14 + 34 = 48 units to space.
Returned to space: 17 + 48 = 65 units = absorbed.
example.answer: 65 units in = 65 units out, so the earth's heat budget balances.

learn.reallife: Monsoon clouds over India release enormous latent heat when vapour condenses into rain, part of the 19 units in the heat budget.

topics.title: Variation in the net heat budget

learn.hook: The tropics get more energy than they lose, and the poles lose more than they get. Without a heat delivery service, the tropics would bake and the poles would freeze solid.
points: The heat budget balances for the whole earth, but not for every latitude.
There is a surplus of net radiation between 40°N and 40°S, and the regions near the poles have a deficit.
The surplus heat from the tropics is redistributed polewards by winds and ocean currents.
As a result, the tropics do not get progressively hotter from accumulating excess heat, and the high latitudes do not get permanently frozen.
NCERT shows this as a graph of net radiation against latitude: positive (surplus) in low latitudes, negative (deficit) towards the poles.

example.q: Kolkata (about 22°N) and a station in Norway (about 70°N): which has a net radiation surplus and which a deficit?
steps: Surplus zone: between 40°N and 40°S.
22°N lies within it → surplus.
70°N lies poleward of 40°N → deficit.
example.answer: Kolkata: surplus; the Norwegian station: deficit.

learn.reallife: Warm ocean currents like the North Atlantic Drift carry tropical heat to north-west Europe, keeping its ports ice-free, an example of heat redistribution.

topics.title: Temperature and the factors controlling it

learn.hook: Mumbai and Nagpur are at almost the same latitude, but Nagpur roasts in May while Mumbai stays milder. Distance from the sea explains a lot.
points: Heat represents the molecular movement of particles in a substance; temperature is the measurement in degrees of how hot or cold a thing or place is.
Factors controlling temperature distribution: (i) latitude, (ii) altitude, (iii) distance from the sea, (iv) air-mass circulation, (v) warm and cold ocean currents, and local aspects.

Latitude: temperature depends on insolation, which varies with latitude. Altitude: the atmosphere is heated from below, so places near sea level are warmer; temperature generally falls with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m.

Distance from the sea: the sea heats and cools slowly; land heats and cools quickly. Places near the sea come under the moderating influence of sea and land breezes, so their temperature range is smaller.
Air masses and ocean currents: places under warm air masses are warmer, those under cold air masses colder. Coasts with warm ocean currents are warmer than coasts with cold currents.

example.q: The temperature at sea level is 30°C. Using the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m, what is the temperature at 2,000 m?
steps: Temperature = 30 − 13 = 17°C.

learn.reallife: Chennai's summer range is smaller than Delhi's partly because sea breezes moderate the coast, while inland Delhi feels the full effect of continentality.

topics.title: Distribution of temperature: January and July isotherms

learn.hook: Draw lines joining places with equal temperature on a world map and they bend in curious ways, revealing hidden warm currents and frozen continents.
points: Isotherms are lines joining places having equal temperature. They are generally parallel to latitudes, showing the effect of latitude; deviations are more pronounced in January than in July, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.

In January (Northern Hemisphere winter), isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent. Warm currents, the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift, make the North Atlantic warmer so isotherms bend north; over Europe and especially the Siberian plain, temperatures fall sharply and isotherms bend south.
January means: over 27°C in equatorial oceans, over 24°C in the tropics, 2°C to 0°C in middle latitudes, and −18°C to −48°C in the Eurasian continental interior.
In the Southern Hemisphere, larger oceans make isotherms more regular and roughly parallel to latitudes; the 20°C, 10°C and 0°C isotherms run along about 35°S, 45°S and 60°S in January.

In July, isotherms generally run parallel to latitudes. Equatorial oceans exceed 27°C; over 30°C is found over subtropical continental Asia along 30°N. The highest annual range of temperature, more than 60°C, is over north-eastern Eurasia, due to continentality; the least range, 3°C, is between 20°S and 15°N.

example.q: On a January map, isotherms over the North Atlantic bend sharply northwards. What does this tell you?
steps: A northward bend means warm temperatures extend to higher latitudes over that area.
In the North Atlantic, the warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift flow north-east.
So the ocean there is warmer than other areas at the same latitude in January.
example.answer: Warm ocean currents (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift) are warming the North Atlantic.

learn.reallife: In January, Srinagar can be below freezing while Thiruvananthapuram stays warm, a gradient you could draw with isotherms across India.

topics.title: Inversion of temperature and air drainage

learn.hook: On winter mornings in Delhi, smog and fog hug the ground and flights get delayed. Above that grey blanket, the air is actually warmer.
points: Normally temperature decreases with height (normal lapse rate). When this is reversed and temperature increases with height, it is called inversion of temperature. Inversions are usually short but quite common; over polar areas, inversion is normal throughout the year.
Ideal conditions: a long winter night with clear skies and still air. The day's heat is radiated off at night, so by early morning the earth is cooler than the air above.

Surface inversion promotes stability in the lower atmosphere. Smoke and dust collect beneath the inversion layer and spread horizontally; dense morning fogs are common, especially in winter. The inversion usually lasts a few hours until the sun warms the earth.

Air drainage: in hills and mountains, cold, dense air formed at night flows downslope under gravity, like water, and piles up in pockets and valley bottoms with warm air above. This is why valley floors get frost while slopes are warmer; it protects plants on the slopes from frost damage.
Exam tip: be ready to explain the heat budget, factors controlling temperature, why subtropics get more insolation than the equator, isotherm patterns and conditions for inversion.

example.q: A farmer in a hill valley plants his orchard on the mid-slope instead of the valley floor. Why is this wise?
steps: On clear, calm nights, cold dense air drains down the slopes.
It collects in the valley bottom, causing frost there.
The mid-slopes stay relatively warmer (inversion).
So orchards on slopes are protected from frost damage.
example.answer: Because air drainage collects frost-forming cold air in the valley floor, while slopes stay warmer.

learn.reallife: Apple orchards in Himachal and tea gardens in Darjeeling are often on slopes rather than valley floors, partly to avoid frost pockets created by air drainage.

chapters.title: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems

topics.title: Atmospheric pressure and its vertical variation

learn.hook: A sealed packet of chips puffs up when you drive up to Mussoorie. The air outside is pressing on it less.
points: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of a column of air contained in a unit area from mean sea level to the top of the atmosphere. It is expressed in millibars (mb).
The average atmospheric pressure at sea level is 1,013.2 mb. Due to gravity, the air at the surface is denser and so has higher pressure.
Pressure is measured with a mercury barometer or an aneroid barometer.
In the lower atmosphere, pressure decreases rapidly with height, by about 1 mb for each 10 m increase in elevation (not always at the same rate).

The vertical pressure gradient force is much larger than the horizontal one, but it is generally balanced by a nearly equal and opposite gravitational force. Hence we do not experience strong upward winds.

example.q: Pressure at sea level is 1,013 mb. Using a fall of about 1 mb per 10 m, estimate the pressure at a hill town 500 m above sea level.
steps: Pressure = 1,013 − 50 = 963 mb.
example.answer: About 963 mb.

learn.reallife: Aircraft altimeters work like aneroid barometers, converting the drop in air pressure into a height reading.

topics.title: Isobars and horizontal distribution of pressure

learn.hook: A weather map full of tightly packed lines over the Bay of Bengal is a warning: a strong wind system is brewing.
points: Small differences in horizontal pressure are highly significant for wind direction and velocity.
Isobars are lines connecting places having equal pressure. To remove the effect of altitude, pressure at every station is reduced to sea level before comparison.
A low-pressure system is enclosed by one or more isobars with the lowest pressure at the centre; a high-pressure system has the highest pressure at the centre.
The pressure gradient is the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong (steep) where isobars are close together and weak (gentle) where isobars are far apart.
Map reading: on world maps of sea-level pressure in January and July, the pressure belts can be traced, and their shift between the two months is visible.

example.q: On a map, isobars over region A are 50 km apart and over region B 200 km apart, with the same pressure interval. Where will winds be stronger?
steps: Closer isobars mean a steeper pressure gradient.
A steeper pressure gradient produces stronger winds.
Region A has isobars closer together.
example.answer: Region A, because its closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient.

learn.reallife: IMD's daily weather charts show isobars; closely spaced isobars around a depression in the Bay of Bengal mean strong winds and a warning for fishermen.

topics.title: World pressure belts and their seasonal shift

learn.hook: The earth wears belts of pressure, alternating low and high from the equator to the poles, and the whole set shifts north and south with the seasons.
points: Near the equator, sea-level pressure is low: the equatorial low (equatorial trough).
Along 30°N and 30°S lie high-pressure areas called the subtropical highs.
Further polewards, along 60°N and 60°S, are low-pressure belts called the subpolar lows. Near the poles the pressure is high: the polar highs.
These pressure belts are not permanent in position. They oscillate with the apparent movement of the sun: in the Northern Hemisphere they move southwards in winter and northwards in summer.

example.q: List the pressure belts you cross flying from the North Pole to the equator.
steps: Start at the pole: polar high.
Around 60°N: subpolar low.
Around 30°N: subtropical high.
At the equator: equatorial low.
example.answer: Polar high → subpolar low (60°N) → subtropical high (30°N) → equatorial low.

learn.reallife: The northward shift of the equatorial low in summer over north India helps pull the south-west monsoon winds into the subcontinent.

topics.title: Forces affecting winds: pressure gradient, friction and Coriolis

learn.hook: Why do cyclones never form right at the equator? Because one invisible force, the Coriolis force, is zero there.
points: Wind is air moving from high pressure to low pressure. Its velocity and direction depend on three forces: the pressure gradient force, the frictional force and the Coriolis force (gravity acts downwards).
Pressure gradient force: the rate of change of pressure with distance. It is strong where isobars are close and weak where they are apart; it acts perpendicular to the isobars.
Frictional force affects wind speed. It is greatest at the surface and its influence generally extends up to 1–3 km. Friction is minimal over the sea surface.

Coriolis force, named after the French physicist who described it in 1844, results from the earth's rotation. It deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. Deflection is more when wind velocity is high.

The Coriolis force is directly proportional to the angle of latitude: maximum at the poles and absent at the equator. At the equator, wind blows perpendicular to the isobars and a low pressure fills up instead of intensifying, which is why tropical cyclones do not form near the equator.

example.q: A wind blows from south to north in the Northern Hemisphere. Which way will the Coriolis force deflect it?
steps: In the Northern Hemisphere, deflection is to the right of the direction of motion.
Facing north, your right is east.
So the wind is deflected towards the east (becoming south-westerly).
example.answer: To the right, i.e., towards the east.

learn.reallife: The south-east trade winds crossing the equator into the Indian Ocean are deflected to the right and arrive in India as the south-west monsoon.

topics.title: Geostrophic wind, cyclonic and anticyclonic circulation

learn.hook: In the Northern Hemisphere, a cyclone spins anticlockwise. Cross the equator, and the same storm would spin clockwise.
points: Winds in the upper atmosphere, 2–3 km above the surface, are free from surface friction and are controlled by the pressure gradient and the Coriolis force.
When isobars are straight and there is no friction, the pressure gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force and the wind blows parallel to the isobars. This is the geostrophic wind.
Wind circulation around a low is cyclonic circulation; around a high it is anticyclonic circulation.

Directions (NCERT table): around a low (cyclone), anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere; around a high (anticyclone), clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Over low-pressure areas, air converges and rises; over high-pressure areas, air subsides from above and diverges at the surface. Rising air (also from eddies, convection, orographic uplift and fronts) is essential for clouds and precipitation.

example.q: A low-pressure system lies over Australia. In which direction do its winds circulate?
steps: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere.
Circulation around a low is cyclonic.
In the Southern Hemisphere, cyclonic circulation is clockwise.
example.answer: Clockwise.

learn.reallife: Satellite images of cyclones hitting Odisha always show an anticlockwise swirl, because the Bay of Bengal is in the Northern Hemisphere.

topics.title: General circulation: ITCZ and the three cells

learn.hook: The atmosphere runs like three giant conveyor belts in each hemisphere, carrying heat from the tropics towards the poles.
points: The pattern of planetary winds depends on: latitudinal variation of heating, emergence of pressure belts, migration of the belts with the sun's apparent path, distribution of continents and oceans, and the earth's rotation.

At the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), high insolation causes convection and low pressure. Winds from the tropics converge here; the air rises to the top of the troposphere (up to about 14 km) and moves polewards.

Hadley cell (tropics): the air accumulates and sinks at about 30°N and S, forming the subtropical high. Near the surface, air flows back towards the equator as the easterlies (trade winds), which converge at the ITCZ.
Ferrel cell (middle latitudes): sinking cold air from the poles and rising warm air from the subtropical high; at the surface the winds are the westerlies.

Polar cell: cold, dense air subsides near the poles and blows towards the middle latitudes as the polar easterlies. These three cells set the pattern of general circulation, and the transfer of heat from lower to higher latitudes maintains it.

example.q: Name the surface winds in each cell of the Northern Hemisphere, from the equator to the pole.
steps: Hadley cell (0°–30°N): easterlies, i.e., the north-east trade winds.
Ferrel cell (30°–60°N): westerlies.
Polar cell (60°–90°N): polar easterlies.
example.answer: Trade winds (easterlies) → westerlies → polar easterlies.

learn.reallife: In July, the ITCZ shifts north over the Ganga plain, part of the system that draws the monsoon into India.

topics.title: El Nino, ENSO and seasonal winds

learn.hook: Warm water appearing off the coast of Peru can mean a weak monsoon in India. The atmosphere and the oceans are deeply linked.
points: The general circulation affects the oceans: large-scale winds start large, slow ocean currents, and oceans in turn supply energy and water vapour to the air.

Warming and cooling of the Pacific Ocean is most important. Warm water of the central Pacific slowly drifts towards the South American coast and replaces the cool Peruvian current. This appearance of warm water off Peru is called El Nino.
El Nino is closely linked with pressure changes in the Central Pacific and Australia; this change in pressure over the Pacific is the Southern Oscillation. The combined phenomenon is ENSO.
In strong ENSO years, the arid west coast of South America gets heavy rain, Australia faces drought (sometimes India too), and China faces floods. ENSO is monitored for long-range forecasting.

Seasonal winds: wind circulation is modified in different seasons by the shift of regions of maximum heating, pressure and wind belts. The most pronounced effect is the monsoon, especially over South-east Asia.

example.q: Why does IMD watch Pacific Ocean temperatures before forecasting India's monsoon?
steps: Warm water off Peru (El Nino) is linked with pressure changes over the Pacific (Southern Oscillation).
Strong ENSO causes large-scale weather variations around the world.
These can include drought in Australia and sometimes in India.
So ENSO helps in long-range monsoon forecasting.
example.answer: Because El Nino/ENSO can weaken India's monsoon, so it is used for long-range forecasting.

learn.reallife: IMD's long-range monsoon forecast each April mentions whether El Nino or La Nina conditions are expected in the Pacific.

topics.title: Local winds: land and sea breezes, mountain and valley winds

learn.hook: On Marina Beach in Chennai, the afternoon sea breeze brings relief. At night, the wind quietly reverses and blows out to sea.
points: Land and sea absorb and transfer heat differently. By day, land heats faster than the sea, so air over land rises and pressure falls, while the cooler sea has relatively high pressure. Wind blows from sea to land: the sea breeze.
At night the reverse happens: land loses heat faster and becomes cooler than the sea, so the pressure gradient is from land to sea, giving a land breeze.

Mountain and valley winds: by day, slopes heat up and air moves upslope, and air from the valley blows up the valley: the valley breeze. At night, slopes cool and dense air descends into the valley as the mountain wind.
Cool air from high plateaus and ice fields draining into valleys is called katabatic wind.

Warm winds occur on the leeward side of mountain ranges: moisture condenses and precipitates on the windward side; the dry air descending the leeward slope is warmed adiabatically and can melt snow quickly. Examples include the Foehn in the Alps and the Chinook in the Rockies.

example.q: At 3 p.m. on a sunny day in Mumbai, which way does the local wind blow? At 3 a.m.?
steps: 3 p.m.: land is warmer than the sea, so low pressure over land.
Wind blows from sea to land → sea breeze.
3 a.m.: land is cooler than the sea, so higher pressure over land.
Wind blows from land to sea → land breeze.
example.answer: 3 p.m.: sea breeze (sea to land); 3 a.m.: land breeze (land to sea).

learn.reallife: Fishermen along the Kerala coast traditionally sail out with the early-morning land breeze and return with the afternoon sea breeze.

topics.title: Air masses and their source regions

learn.hook: A cold wave that sweeps into north India in January carries the 'personality' of the frozen lands where its air was born.
points: When air stays over a homogeneous area (a vast ocean or plain) long enough, it acquires the characteristics of that area. Air with distinctive temperature and humidity is an air mass: a large body of air with little horizontal variation in temperature and moisture.
The homogeneous surfaces over which air masses form are their source regions. Air masses are classified by source region.

Five major source regions: (i) warm tropical and subtropical oceans; (ii) subtropical hot deserts; (iii) relatively cold high-latitude oceans; (iv) very cold snow-covered continents in high latitudes; (v) permanently ice-covered continents in the Arctic and Antarctica.
Types: maritime tropical (mT), continental tropical (cT), maritime polar (mP), continental polar (cP) and continental arctic (cA).
Tropical air masses are warm; polar air masses are cold. Maritime ones are moist; continental ones are dry.

example.q: Classify an air mass formed over the hot Sahara desert.
steps: Over land → continental (c).
Hot subtropical desert → tropical (T).
So it is continental tropical (cT): warm and dry.
example.answer: Continental tropical (cT), warm and dry.

learn.reallife: Moist maritime tropical air from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal feeds India's monsoon, while dry continental air dominates its winter.
